title: Draining another statement's results is unbounded in memory and is triggered by every commit/rollback
evidence: `drain_into_buffer` calls `fill_pending(client, &mut state, usize::MAX, usize::MAX);` (line 206) and, for each later result, `read_rows_into(client, &mut rows, ..., usize::MAX, usize::MAX)` (lines 225-232). `Connection::client_op` runs `release_wire(&mut slot, 0)` before every commit/rollback/set_attr (connection.rs:~129-133), and `close()` does the same (connection.rs:~234). The pattern `cur.execute('SELECT ... huge'); for row in cur: ...; conn.commit()` therefore buffers the entire remaining result set into RAM at the first commit. The fetch paths cap batches (`FETCH_BATCH_BYTES` = 16 MiB), but the drain path caps nothing. The same applies when a second cursor executes on the connection.
fix: Cap the drain with a byte budget (for example 64 MiB, configurable). When it is exceeded, stop reading and mark the owner's result as `Failed(HY000 'result set discarded: connection needed by another statement')`, or spill to a temp file, instead of growing without bound. Document the chosen behaviour in ARCHITECTURE.md's MARS section. For `close()` and `Connection::close` there is no reason to drain at all: `release_wire` should discard the owner's rows, because the connection is going away.
verify:
The code matches the finding. `drain_into_buffer` (statement.rs:206 and 225-232) reads with `usize::MAX` row and byte limits. `release_wire(&mut slot, 0)` calls it from `client_op` (connection.rs:133) and from `close()` (connection.rs:235). `release_wire` drains whenever the owner's weak reference is still alive and its id differs from the requester, and the requester id 0 never matches a statement id. So commit, rollback, set_attr or close with a live, partly fetched cursor buffers the whole remaining result set in RAM. docs/ARCHITECTURE.md (MARS section, lines 78-85) documents the draining but not any size limit, and docs/CONTRACT.md says nothing about it.

I would downgrade it from blocking to should-fix, for these reasons:
- The unbounded buffering is a deliberate design choice, documented as emulating msodbcsql with MARS. A cap that fails the owner's result would change behaviour that upstream tests may rely on.
- Real drivers also buffer or block in this case, and the pattern (commit in the middle of iterating a huge result) is uncommon.
- It is a memory and latency risk, not a correctness bug on common paths.

The part of the fix that is clearly worth doing is for close. In `Connection::close` the connection is going away, so draining is pure waste. It also reads the entire remaining result over the network before the pool or socket is released. The code already has the discard path (`close_query`). For close, `release_wire` should discard instead of drain. Treat a byte cap or a spill file for commit and rollback as optional hardening, and document the chosen behaviour in ARCHITECTURE.md.

title: Locks taken with the GIL held, contradicting the documented lock model; getinfo can hang every Python thread
evidence: statement.rs:4-8 and ARCHITECTURE.md say 'Both locks are only ever taken with the GIL released (`py.detach`)'. But `get_info` does `let slot = conn.slot.lock();` with no detach (getinfo.rs:24), and `Connection::get_info` calls it directly (connection.rs:~329). `slot` is held for the whole network duration of any execute or fetch on another thread. Thread A runs a long query and holds `slot`. Thread B calls `conn.getinfo(...)`, which blocks inside `slot.lock()` while holding the GIL. Thread C can no longer reach `cursor.cancel()` or `_cancel`, so nothing can unblock the query. The same GIL-held `state.lock()` pattern appears in statement.rs:577, 712, 740 (`row_count`), 747 (`num_result_cols`), 760 (`describe_col`), 857, 933, 958, 968, 991 and 1002. These block on `StmtShared::state`, which `fetch` and `drain_into_buffer` hold across network reads.
fix: Either honour the rule or change it. Cheapest: keep an `ArcSwap`/`parking_lot::RwLock` snapshot (`columns`, `rowcount`, `diag`, server_version/database/name) that is updated at the end of each operation, so the metadata getters never touch `slot` or `state`. Alternatively wrap those getters in `py.detach`. Then correct the doc comment. Add a threading test: thread A runs `WAITFOR DELAY '00:00:10'` and thread B calls `conn.getinfo(...)`, which must return immediately.
verify: Confirmed. getinfo.rs:24 does `conn.slot.lock()` with the GIL held. Connection::get_info (connection.rs:329-333) calls it with no `py.detach`. The `slot` lock is held across network I/O elsewhere: statement.rs:519 and 875 take it inside detach, and 369/460/610 take it too. So `getinfo` on one thread blocks while holding the GIL until another thread's query finishes. The same pattern is in statement.rs `state.lock()` at 740 (row_count), 747 (num_result_cols), 760 (describe_col), 857, 933, 937, 958, 968, 991 and 1002. Both the statement.rs:6-8 header and ARCHITECTURE.md:70-72 claim both locks are only taken with the GIL released, so the docs are wrong as written. Nothing in CONTRACT.md or upstream compatibility requires this behaviour. Two caveats: (1) it is a stall, not a true deadlock, because the lock holder never needs the GIL while it holds the lock, so it ends when the query ends. (2) The "cancel unreachable" part is speculative, since I found no cancel path in connection.rs, and it only matters if cancel goes through the GIL or the same locks. The trigger needs concurrent use of one connection from several threads, which is uncommon. Grade should-fix, not blocking. The cheap fix is to wrap the getters in `py.detach`, or to cache server_version, database and name at connect time. Either way, correct the doc comment.

title: Deferred session SQL is dropped when it fails (isolation level / USE db silently lost)
evidence: `prepare_session` does `let mut session = conn.take_pending_session_sql();` (statement.rs:343), and `take_pending_session_sql` uses `std::mem::take(&mut *pending).join("; ")` (connection.rs:69-72), which empties the queue before the SQL runs. If the batch then fails (timeout, transient error, cancel), `return Err(diag::records_for_error(&err, "HY000"))` (line 359) leaves the queue empty. `implicit_transactions` is correctly not updated on failure, but the `SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL` / `USE [db]` from `attrs_before` is gone, and the next execute runs at the wrong isolation level or in the wrong database with no error. The parameter `handle: &CancelHandle` is also unused (`let _ = handle;`, line 363), so a cancel does not reach this batch.
fix: Peek instead of take: clear `pending_session_sql` only after the batch succeeds, or re-queue on error. Pass `ExecuteOptions::new().timeout_secs(timeout).cancel(handle)` into the session batch, or drop the parameter.
verify: Confirmed in the code. `prepare_session` (statement.rs:343) calls `conn.take_pending_session_sql()`, which empties the queue with `std::mem::take(...).join("; ")` (connection.rs:69-72). On batch failure it returns Err at line 359, so the queue stays empty. Nothing else re-queues it. The only writer is construction at connection.rs:219, and `run_session_sql` at lines 301/305 runs later `attrs_before` changes immediately instead. `set_implicit_transactions` is correctly skipped on failure, so IMPLICIT_TRANSACTIONS is retried, but the isolation-level and `USE db` statements from connect-time attrs_before are lost. A timeout or transient error on the first statement means a retry on the same connection silently runs at the default isolation level or in the wrong database. `handle` is also unused (`let _ = handle;`), as the finding says. Nothing in docs/CONTRACT.md or upstream compatibility argues against changing this. The fix is small and local: re-queue the session SQL on error, or clear it only after success. It is not blocking, because it needs a failed first statement on a connection that is then reused. I kept should-fix because the failure is silent and changes transaction semantics. The cancel-handle half is a minor nit.

title: translate_call_escape can panic on non-ASCII SQL, and conversion_error classifies by substring
evidence: `if rest.len() < 4 || !rest[..4].eq_ignore_ascii_case("call")` slices a `&str` at byte 4. For SQL such as `{abcé}` (`trim` starts with '{' and ends with '}', `rest` = "abcé", len 5) the byte index 4 falls inside 'é' and the slice panics. In PyO3 that surfaces as `pyo3_runtime.PanicException`, which derives from BaseException, so it bypasses `except Exception`. This contradicts ARCHITECTURE.md ('never panic'). `exec_direct` and `rewrite_qmarks` both call it on arbitrary user SQL. Separately, `params::conversion_error` (params/mod.rs:93-104) picks ValueError vs TypeError with `lower.contains("precision")` / `contains("range")` / `contains("overflow")` on the mssql-tds error text, so a dependency wording change silently flips exception types.
fix: Use `rest.get(..4).is_some_and(|p| p.eq_ignore_ascii_case("call"))`. Add a unit test with a multi-byte character in the escape. For `conversion_error`, match on the `mssql_tds::error::Error` variants if they exist, or have `py_types` return its own small error enum (`OutOfRange`, `Unsupported`, `PrecisionTooHigh`) that is mapped once.
verify: Confirmed in src/params/placeholders.rs:20. `rest[..4]` slices a &str at byte 4 with no char-boundary check. `rest` is whatever follows `{` (and an optional `? =`), and `translate_call_escape` runs on arbitrary user SQL from statement.rs:556 (exec_direct) and rewrite_qmarks. Input `{abcé}` has `é` at bytes 3-4, so the slice panics. A more realistic input such as `{fn ç...}` or `{ts 'é'}` hits the same boundary. A PyO3 panic becomes PanicException, which derives from BaseException and bypasses `except Exception`. That contradicts the "never panic" rule in ARCHITECTURE.md, and nothing elsewhere guards against it. The trigger is narrow, since the SQL must start with `{` and end with `}` and have a multi-byte character at that position. The fix is a one-line `rest.get(..4).is_some_and(|p| p.eq_ignore_ascii_case("call"))`, so I grade it should-fix. The second half of the finding is a nit. `conversion_error` does match on error-message substrings, which is fragile to dependency wording changes, but it only picks between ValueError and TypeError, and a structured error enum is real churn. Fix it only if mssql_tds exposes variants cheaply.

title: Lock-order and GIL rule from ARCHITECTURE.md is violated: state/slot locks taken with the GIL held
evidence: ARCHITECTURE.md: "Both are taken only with the GIL released (`py.detach`)". But `row_count` does `Ok(stmt_of(statement_handle)?.state.lock().rowcount)`, `num_result_cols`, `describe_col` (`stmt.state.lock().columns.clone()`), `check_error`, `get_all_diag_records`, `set_stmt_attr`, `not_implemented` all lock `StmtShared::state` with no `py.detach`. `fetch()` (line 459) holds `slot` and `state` across `fill_pending` -> `block_on` network I/O. `getinfo.rs:21` does `conn.slot.lock()` with the GIL held too.
fix: Either wrap those short lock sections in `py.detach`, or have `fetch`/`execute_command` not hold `state` across `block_on` (publish `rowcount`/`columns`/`diag` through an atomic or a separate small mutex). Otherwise a Python thread polling `cursor.rowcount`, `get_info`, or a watchdog calling `DDBCSQLCheckError` freezes the whole interpreter for the duration of a long fetch. Update ARCHITECTURE.md if the rule is deliberately relaxed.
verify: Confirmed in code. ARCHITECTURE.md (lines 70-72) and the module doc in statement.rs (lines 6-8) say both locks are only taken with the GIL released. In fact `row_count` (line 740), `num_result_cols` (747), `describe_col` (760), and the diag, attr and not_implemented paths (933-1031) call `stmt.state.lock()` with the GIL held. `get_info` in getinfo.rs:21 does the same with `conn.slot.lock()`. `fetch()` (459-461) takes `slot` and `state` and keeps them across `fill_pending`, which does network I/O. It runs inside `py.detach`, so the GIL is released and other threads can run. If another thread then calls one of the GIL-holding paths on the same statement or connection, it blocks on the parking_lot mutex while holding the GIL. That freezes every Python thread for the length of the network read. It is a stall, not a deadlock: `fetch` drops its locks before the GIL is reacquired, so the waiter proceeds once I/O finishes. The trigger needs two threads sharing one cursor or connection, which upstream tolerates because ODBC releases the GIL around blocking calls. That is uncommon, so this is not blocking. The cheapest fix is to wrap the short lock sections in `py.detach`, or else relax the documented rule.

title: fetchmany(n) silently returns fewer than n rows when the 16 MiB read-ahead cap is hit
evidence: `fetch()` does `let want = readahead.max(n) - state.pending_rows(); fill_pending(client, &mut state, want, FETCH_BATCH_BYTES);` and `read_rows_into` stops when `bytes_written(sink) < max_bytes` is false (`FETCH_BATCH_BYTES = 16 << 20`, `byte_size = cells.len()*size_of::<Cell>() + arena.len()`). `fetch_many` (line 809) calls `fetch(&stmt, fetchSize, fetchSize)` once and returns `SQL_SUCCESS`, and the vendored cursor.fetchmany makes a single DDBCSQLFetchMany call. The cap is meant for fetchall batching, but it also applies here, so fetchmany(100_000) on a 10-column table (about 400 B/row of Cell) returns about 40k rows with no end-of-data signal.
fix: For fetchmany and fetchone, ignore the byte cap and keep reading until `n` rows are buffered or the result ends (pass `usize::MAX` bytes, or loop `fill_pending` until `pending_rows() >= n || result_done`). Keep the cap only in the fetchall loop, where short batches are expected. Add a test that fetchmany(N) returns N rows for wide and for narrow rows.
verify: Confirmed in src/statement.rs. fetch() (line 459) calls fill_pending once at line 478 with FETCH_BATCH_BYTES (16 MiB). read_rows_into stops when bytes_written >= max_bytes even if fewer than n rows are buffered. fetch_many (line 798) passes fetchSize as both n and readahead and makes a single call. It returns SQL_SUCCESS, or SQL_SUCCESS_WITH_INFO if info was recorded. When rows is non-empty it never gives SQL_NO_DATA. So fetchmany(N) can return fewer than N rows mid-result, and nothing tells the caller it is a short batch. fetch_all is safe because it loops. fetchone is unaffected because n=1 always reads at least one row. Nothing in docs/CONTRACT.md allows short fetchmany batches. Upstream ODBC fetches exactly N rows unless the result ends, so this is an upstream-compat deviation; tests or callers that assert len == N, or that treat a short batch as end-of-data, would break. Severity is should-fix, not blocking: DB-API clients that loop until an empty list still work, nothing is lost or corrupted, and the shortfall only appears for very large fetchSize (about 100k rows or more on wide rows). The fix is small. Pass usize::MAX as max_bytes when called from fetch_many (add a byte-cap parameter to fetch), or loop fill_pending until pending_rows() >= n or result_done.

title: Discarding or re-executing a half-read cursor drains the whole remaining result over the wire
evidence: `release_wire` ends with `if client.has_open_batch() { let _ = block_on(client.close_query()); ... }`. It is called from `execute_command`, `close_cursor` (line 520-522) and `client_op` (commit, rollback, close). In mssql-tds, `close_query` loops `advance_to_rows()` and reads every remaining token, so `SELECT * FROM big; fetchone(); cursor.close()` (or a second execute on the same cursor, or conn.close()) reads and decodes the entire result set. The path is neither cancellable nor time-limited, and it runs while holding `slot`, which blocks every other cursor on the connection.
fix: When the statement being discarded is the owner, call `handle.cancel()` on its stored `CancelHandle` (`stmt.cancel`) before `close_query`, so the client sends a TDS attention and drains only to the ACK. Do the same for the `requester==0` paths. Add a test: execute a billion-row SELECT, fetchone, close, and assert it returns in under 1 s.
verify: Confirmed. `release_wire` (src/statement.rs:253-269) ends with `block_on(client.close_query())` whenever `has_open_batch()`. In the pinned mssql-tds (6b6b48e), `close_query` loops `advance_to_rows()` until it returns false, so it reads and decodes every remaining token. It does not send a TDS attention. `release_wire` is called from `execute_command` (370), `close_cursor` (521), the rpc path (611) and `connection.rs` (133, 235: commit, rollback, close), all under the `slot` lock. docs/ARCHITECTURE.md describes only the drain-into-buffer case for another live statement and says nothing about draining a discarded owner, so the docs do not justify this path. The `CancelHandle` for the owning statement already exists in `stmt.cancel` (set at lines 383 and 620), so the fix is available. Cancelling before `close_query` matches ODBC behavior for closing a cursor with pending rows and doesn't conflict with upstream compatibility. Caveats: (1) the `id != requester` case must still buffer, since those rows are wanted, so the fix applies only when the owner is being discarded. (2) The `requester==0` path, with a dead weak owner, has no handle unless the handle is stored in `Slot`. (3) Bytes already in flight are still read until the attention ACK, so the "under 1 s" test is achievable but the cost is not zero. This is a latency and blocking problem, not data corruption or wrong results, so I rate it should-fix, not blocking. I did not run the cancel path against a server.

title: drain_into_buffer is unbounded in memory and can spin if advance() keeps failing with the batch open
evidence: `fill_pending(client, &mut state, usize::MAX, usize::MAX)` and the `Rows` arm's `read_rows_into(..., usize::MAX, usize::MAX)` buffer the whole remaining batch in RAM whenever another statement or a commit needs the wire. In the loop, `Err(err) => { state.queued.push_back(BufferedResult{..error..}); }` has no `break`. It relies on `client.has_open_batch()` turning false, and the `loop { if !client.has_open_batch() { break; } let advanced = block_on(client.advance()); ...` structure has no other exit. If the socket dies or a timeout fires without the client clearing `has_open_batch`, this loop pushes errors forever while holding `slot`.
fix: `break` after the first `Err` from `advance()`, and check `client.is_connection_dead()` each iteration. Cap drained bytes per result (for example, spill to the existing error path above a configurable limit and cancel the rest). Add a test that kills the server connection mid-drain.
verify: Confirmed in src/statement.rs:201-250. The `Err(err)` arm of `client.advance()` pushes a BufferedResult and has no `break`. The only exits are `has_open_batch()` turning false or `StatementResult::End`. In mssql-tds (rev 6b6b48e), `advance()` returns `Err` from `drain_rows` or `position_on_first_result` and I found no code that clears `has_open_batch` on those paths. Only the success and explicit close paths call `set_has_open_batch(false)`. A mid-drain IO failure (dead socket, timeout) therefore leaves the batch open, and the next `advance()` fails again. The loop then spins and pushes error results into `state.queued` without bound while the connection slot stays locked. A `Rows` result that errors mid-read (the `.err()` path) hits the same loop on the next `advance()`. I could not run a dead-socket test to prove that `advance()` keeps erroring, but the code makes it very likely. Nothing in docs/CONTRACT.md or upstream compatibility requires the loop to continue after an error, so adding `break` on the first `advance()` error is safe and cheap. I did not check whether `release_wire`'s later `close_query` copes with a dead connection. The unbounded `usize::MAX` buffering is a real memory cost, but it is inherent to the buffer-on-handoff design, so I would not churn it. I rate this should-fix rather than blocking because it only triggers on connection failure. The fix is to `break` after the first `Err` and add a test that kills the connection mid-drain.

title: Process-wide tokio runtime is not fork-safe
evidence: `static RUNTIME: OnceLock<Runtime>` is built once with `new_multi_thread().worker_threads(..)`. There is no `pthread_atfork` or `os.register_at_fork` handling anywhere in `src/` or `python/mssql_python`. After `os.fork()` (multiprocessing's default on Linux before 3.14, or a gunicorn `--preload` worker) in a process that has already connected, the child inherits the `Runtime` handle but none of its worker threads. Because `block_on` relies on the workers to drive the socket I/O driver, the first connect or query in the child hangs. Pooled `TdsClient`s in `IDLE` are also shared with the parent's sockets.
fix: Register an at-fork child hook (`libc::pthread_atfork`, or `os.register_at_fork(after_in_child=...)` called from module init) that leaks the old runtime and clears `IDLE`. This needs the runtime held in a resettable `Mutex<Option<Arc<Runtime>>>` instead of `OnceLock`. Alternatively, record the creating pid in the runtime and rebuild it when `getpid()` differs.
verify:
Confirmed in the code, not hand-run. src/runtime.rs:13 holds the runtime in a `static OnceLock<Runtime>`, a multi-thread runtime with named worker threads. `block_on` just calls `runtime().block_on`. A grep of src/ and python/mssql_python finds no `pthread_atfork` and no `register_at_fork`. The only `getpid` hits are in logging.py. The grep over docs/*.md for "fork" returned nothing, so CONTRACT.md does not address it either. Nothing elsewhere handles it, and nothing in the docs excuses it.

After a fork, the child inherits the runtime handle but not its worker threads. Spawned tasks and the I/O driver, which worker threads drive, are then dead, so a connect or query in the child will most likely hang. I did not reproduce the hang. The IDLE pool in src/pooling.rs:20 is also inherited, so the child and parent would share live TDS sockets.

This only bites when the runtime was initialised before the fork, for example `multiprocessing` with the fork start method after a connect. Fresh children that never touched the runtime are fine. That limits the severity. Upstream's ODBC layer can open new connections in a forked child, so the Rust port is a behavioural regression against a drop-in replacement. It is not a blocker because it is an uncommon pattern, and sharing live connections across a fork is unsafe in general.

Fix: the pid-check approach is the least churn. Store the creating pid and rebuild the runtime when `getpid()` differs. Pair that with clearing IDLE (leak the inherited clients rather than dropping them) in the child.

title: Malformed access token silently falls back to another auth method
evidence: `decode_access_token` returns `None` for a short buffer, odd UTF-16 or invalid UTF-16. `Connection::new` (connection.rs:175-177) also ignores a token value that is not `bytes` (`if let Ok(bytes) = value.cast::<PyBytes>()`). `build_context` then takes the `else if ... trusted_connection` branch (SSPI) or `TdsAuthenticationMethod::Password` with whatever `Uid`/`Pwd`/`Trusted_Connection` is in the string (connstr.rs:157-168). A caller who supplied a token never gets an error and silently authenticates a different way, for example as the integrated-security identity.
fix: In `Connection::new`, return a `HY000`/`28000` error if `SQL_COPT_SS_ACCESS_TOKEN` is present but is not bytes or does not decode. Also reject the combination of an access token with a non-empty `Pwd` or `Trusted_Connection`.
verify: Confirmed in code. connection.rs:174-178 only sets access_token if the value is PyBytes and decode_access_token returns Some. A non-bytes value, a buffer shorter than 4 bytes, odd-length UTF-16 or invalid UTF-16 all leave it None with no error. The code then falls through to SSPI or Password at connstr.rs:157-168. Nothing else handles this, and docs/CONTRACT.md says nothing that would require it. Raising an error also matches ODBC, which fails on a malformed token. Upstream's Python layer builds the token with get_token_struct, so a malformed token needs hand-built attrs_before. Because of that, and because the failure is an auth error and not a data-loss bug, I rate it should-fix, not blocking. The first half of the proposed fix is worth doing: error when the attribute is present but invalid. The second half, rejecting a token combined with Pwd or Trusted_Connection, is optional. build_context already clears the user name and password when a token is present, so it can be left alone to avoid churn.

title: normalize_column is a 100+ line if-chain with four copy-pasted branches
evidence: One fn handles int, float, text, binary, decimal; each branch repeats `for r in 0..rows.len() { ... std::mem::replace(&mut rows[r][col], SqlType::Bit(None)) ... }`. The text and binary branches both fold max_len with `max_len = match (max_len, X_len(..).unwrap()) {..}`.
fix: Split into normalize_int / normalize_float / normalize_text / normalize_binary / normalize_decimal, each returning bool, and have normalize_column try them in order. Extract a shared `widest_len(values, len_fn, limit)` helper for the text and binary max-length fold.
verify: Confirmed at src/params/batch.rs lines 118-244. `normalize_column` is about 125 lines and runs an ordered chain of int, float, text, binary and decimal strategies, with a fallback for everything else. Splitting it would improve readability, and nothing in CONTRACT or upstream compatibility prevents it, since this is internal Rust with no upstream counterpart. The finding overstates the duplication, though. The branches are not four copies of one loop. Each loop does a different per-cell conversion (int width and Bit, Float, text variant selection, binary, decimal reformat). Only the `for r in 0..rows.len()` / `std::mem::replace` skeleton repeats, and that appears in just two branches (text, binary). The proposed `widest_len` helper would have to cover two slightly different folds. Text caps the length at `limit` (4000 or 8000) and falls back to None above it. Binary has no cap. So a helper needs a limit parameter, or an Option<limit>, to avoid changing behaviour. Control flow is flat, with early returns and no nesting beyond one level. Doc comments state the intent. The function is tested indirectly through the batch paths. Splitting it is optional cleanup that carries a small risk of behaviour drift, and it does not need to block anything. Downgraded from should-fix to nit.

title: Check-then-unwrap pattern: predicate called, then the same Option unwrapped
evidence: `values.iter().all(|&r| text_len(..).is_some())` is followed by `text_len(&rows[r][col]).unwrap()`. The decimal branch does the same: `decimal_parts(&rows[r][col]).unwrap()` at lines 202, 206 and 217, plus `.max().unwrap()` at 129 and 210. The invariant is implicit, so a later edit to one branch can turn it into a panic across the FFI boundary.
fix: Collect `Option<Vec<_>>` once (`let lens: Option<Vec<_>> = values.iter().map(|&r| text_len(..)).collect()`) and use the extracted values, so there is no unwrap and no second lookup.
verify: The pattern is real in src/params/batch.rs. Line ~160 has `all(text_len(..).is_some())` followed by `text_len(..).unwrap()` in the same branch. The binary branch does the same with `binary_len`. The decimal branch calls `decimal_parts(..).unwrap()` after its `all(...)` guard. There are also `.max().unwrap()` calls after `any_int` and after the non-empty `values` check. Every unwrap is currently guarded and cannot fire. The `max()` calls run over a non-empty iterator: `values` is non-empty because of the early `first` return, and the int branch is guarded by `any_int`. The risk is therefore only that a later edit breaks the invariant. A panic would not be undefined behaviour across the FFI boundary, because PyO3 turns it into a PanicException. Nothing in CONTRACT.md or upstream compatibility argues against changing it. The suggested `Option<Vec<_>>` collect is a modest tidy-up that would also remove the repeated lookups, but it is not worth more than a nit. The severity "should-fix" is too high.

title: Silent error swallowing in decimal re-encode
evidence: `match DecimalParts::from_string(&text, precision, scale) { Ok(p) => SqlType::Decimal(Some(p)), Err(_) => continue, }`. On error the cell silently keeps its old, differently scaled value, which breaks the column-uniform type this function exists to guarantee.
fix: Make normalize_column return Result and propagate the error (or fall back to the whole column's untyped path). Never `continue` past a failed conversion.
verify: Confirmed at src/params/batch.rs:216-223. `Err(_) => continue` leaves that cell as its original Decimal, so the column ends up with mixed precision/scale. Nothing else handles it, and docs/CONTRACT.md doesn't require this behavior. The branch is reachable only when the unclamped precision (max integer digits + max scale) exceeds 38. For example, mixing decimal(38,0) with decimal(38,10) clamps the precision to 38, and `from_string` then rejects the 38-digit integer at scale 10. Ordinary inputs always fit, since the target precision is computed to cover every value. The swallow is real but rare. The user-visible symptom would be a bind error or truncation on a pathological batch, not silent wrong data in normal use. Fixing it is cheap: make `normalize_column` return `Result`, or fall back to the untyped path when the clamp bites. It is not should-fix because the trigger is very narrow.

title: execute_command is a 90+ line function mixing locking, session setup, null resolution, execution, result mapping and read-ahead
evidence: One body holds `conn.slot.lock()`, `prepare_session`, `resolve_null_types`, the `block_on` match, the StatementResult-to-state mapping, and `fill_pending(..)` with the error-swap `std::mem::take(&mut state.diag)`. `let ret = if ret == SQL_SUCCESS && state.columns.is_some() { ... } else { ret }` shadows `ret` twice.
fix: Extract `run_command(client, command, ..) -> Result<StatementResult, Error>`, `apply_result(state, client, result) -> SqlReturn` and `surface_first_row_error(state) -> SqlReturn`. Leave execute_command as the outline.
verify: The structure matches the finding, but the size is overstated. execute_command runs from line 367 to about 442, roughly 76 lines, not 90+. It is a linear, well-commented sequence: lock, session setup, null resolution, execute, map result, read-ahead. Nothing is duplicated, and docs/CONTRACT.md and upstream compatibility don't constrain it. `ret` is shadowed twice. The error-swap block that uses `std::mem::take(&mut state.diag)` is the densest part. An `apply_result` or `surface_first_row_error` helper could be extracted there. The proposed `run_command` helper is awkward because `client`, `slot` and `state` are all held under locks acquired in a fixed order. Splitting adds borrow-passing churn for little gain. It is a style nit, not should-fix.

title: execute_batch has the same shape: 95 lines, nested loop, inline error-record plumbing
evidence: It does lock/reset, null probing (`let mut probe = ParamSet {..}`), a chunk-drain loop that builds RpcParameters with `format!("@P{}", j + 1)`, then per-row error conversion (`state.diag.insert(0, DiagRecord::new(diag::sqlstate_for_server_error(..)..`), then cleanup. The `Err` arm hand-rolls prepend with `records.append(&mut state.diag)`. The setup prefix is the same as execute_command (clear diag, reset_results, `not_connected()`, CancelHandle).
fix: Extract `resolve_batch_null_types(..)`, `build_chunk_params(chunk, base)`, `server_errors_to_records(&batch)` and a shared `begin_statement(stmt) -> Result<(guards, handle), SqlReturn>` used by both execute paths.
verify: The code matches the description. execute_batch is about 95 lines. It inlines the null-type probe, the RpcParameter construction with format!("@P{}"), and the server-error to DiagRecord conversion. The Err arm does the manual `records.append(&mut state.diag)`. The setup prefix (release_wire, lock, diag.clear, reset_results, not_connected, CancelHandle, prepare_session) is duplicated from execute_command. The finding overreaches in two places. First, the nesting is shallow: one while loop with a match, not deeply nested, and the function reads linearly. Second, the proposed shared `begin_statement(stmt) -> (guards, handle)` is awkward in Rust. `client` is a &mut borrowed from the `slot` guard, so a helper would have to return the guards plus a borrow, or use a closure. The two paths also differ: execute_command checks `state.freed` and execute_batch does not. Nothing in docs/CONTRACT.md or upstream compatibility rules out the extraction, but it is a pure readability refactor with no correctness impact. The small pure helpers (build_chunk_params, server_errors_to_records, null resolution) are cheap and reasonable. The shared begin helper is not worth the churn. Overall this is a nit, not should-fix.

title: Dead parameters and no-op `let _ =` used to silence warnings
evidence: `let _ = handle;` (363) and `let _ = handle_type;` (978); `#[allow(non_snake_case, unused_variables)]` on SQLExecuteMany/others (562, 698, 745, 752) and `#[allow(unused_variables)]` on `Connection::new` (`token_factory`).
fix: Prefix intentionally unused pyo3 args with `_` (pyo3 `signature` keeps the Python name) or drop the parameter. Remove the `let _ = x;` lines and the blanket unused_variables allows so the compiler flags real dead code.
verify: Confirmed in the code. `let _ = handle;` is at statement.rs:363 and `let _ = handle_type;` is at 978. Blanket `#[allow(non_snake_case, unused_variables)]` sits on `execute` (562) and several others, and `#[allow(unused_variables)]` is on `Connection::new` (connection.rs:155). The camelCase parameter names (statementHandle and so on) and the unused arguments are there to mirror the upstream ddbc_bindings signature, which the pyo3 `signature` attributes preserve. So the unused parameters are deliberate, not a bug. The fix is cosmetic: prefix with `_` or narrow the allows to the specific parameters. The blanket allow can hide a real unused variable in those functions, but nothing is wrong today. Not blocking and low value, so keep it as a nit.

title: bench_taxi.py: run_mssql_python is one function with ten nested closures, and timed() catches bare Exception
evidence: `except Exception as exc:  # a driver that lacks a feature still reports the rest` swallows every failure, including bugs in the benchmark itself; `run_mssql_python` defines fetchall_100k ... duckdb_over_arrow_3m as nested defs (lines 62-119) and `run_fastmssql` repeats the pattern.
fix: Hoist the workloads to module-level functions taking a connection, in a `WORKLOADS = {name: fn}` table shared by both drivers. In `timed`, catch only NotImplementedError/AttributeError for 'feature missing' and record the exception type in the result so real failures are visible.
verify: The code matches the finding. timed() catches bare Exception around the warm-up call only, and run_mssql_python defines about ten nested closures (lines 62-119). run_fastmssql repeats the pattern with four. The catch is deliberate and commented: a driver that lacks a feature still reports the other workloads, and the error is recorded in the result as "Type: message" (truncated to 200 chars). So the failure is visible in the output and not silently swallowed. The finding's suggestion to record the exception type is therefore already done. Narrowing the catch to NotImplementedError/AttributeError would be wrong for a cross-driver benchmark: other drivers raise driver-specific errors (ProgrammingError, etc.) for unsupported features. The nested closures are a cosmetic style choice. They share conn/cs through closure scope, and hoisting them would force a table of connection-taking functions for a throwaway script. Nothing in CONTRACT.md or upstream compatibility bears on it. Only a weak residue remains: the warm-up failure might hide a bug in the benchmark itself, though it is still reported as an error entry. This is a nit at most, with low value to fix.

title: statement.rs is a god module: ODBC facade, wire-ownership scheduler, fetch buffering and executemany in one file
evidence: 1036 lines mix five concerns: (a) pyfunction facade (exec_direct, fetch_one, describe_col, check_error ~L554-1000); (b) MARS emulation (release_wire L253, drain_into_buffer L201, BufferedResult L48); (c) cursor/result state machine (StmtState L57, more_results L872); (d) execute pipeline (execute_command L367, prepare_session L334, resolve_null_types L284); (e) executemany (execute_batch L603). Only 4 files in src/ have #[cfg(test)] and none touch statement.rs, because every path requires Py<>/TdsClient. Catalog also reaches in via map_columns/exec_catalog_rpc.
fix: Split into: `session/` (Slot + owner + release_wire + drain: the 'who owns the wire' module, moved out of connection.rs/statement.rs), `cursor.rs` (StmtState: pending/queued/take_pending/more_results logic, pure Rust), `exec.rs` (execute_command, execute_batch, prepare_session), and a thin `odbc_api.rs` holding only #[pyfunction]s that unwrap handles, call the Rust-only modules, and convert to Python. Facade stays shallow by design; behaviour moves behind deeper modules.
verify:
The facts check out. src/statement.rs is 1036 lines and holds the pyfunction facade, release_wire/drain_into_buffer (MARS emulation), StmtState and BufferedResult, execute_command and prepare_session, and execute_batch. connection.rs imports release_wire and StmtShared from statement.rs, while statement.rs depends on connection's Slot and ConnShared. catalog.rs also reaches in through map_columns, exec_catalog_rpc and exec_catalog_query. That is a real, if mild, circular coupling.

Several things weigh against a higher grade. docs/ARCHITECTURE.md deliberately lists statement.rs as the one owner of the execute/fetch/more-results state machine, MARS emulation and executemany. The code is tightly bound to Py<> and TdsClient, so splitting it does not make it unit-testable by itself. A 1000-line Rust file is not unusual. Nothing in docs/CONTRACT.md or upstream compatibility is affected, since the pyfunction surface would not change.

The split is a maintainability suggestion with moderate churn and no correctness or performance gain. The cheapest useful step would be to move the wire-ownership code (Slot, release_wire, drain_into_buffer) next to connection.rs to break the cycle. The full four-way split is not worth doing now, so this is a nit rather than should-fix.

title: No seam between statement logic and TdsClient; MARS/fetch/readahead logic cannot be tested without a SQL Server
evidence: `fn fill_pending(client: &mut TdsClient, state: &mut StmtState, ...)`, `drain_into_buffer(other, client: &mut TdsClient)`, `release_wire(slot: &mut Slot, ...)` all take the concrete mssql_tds::TdsClient and call block_on inside. The trickiest invariants (on_wire/result_done/pending_error/owner transitions, read-ahead error ordering) have zero unit tests; `cargo test --lib` only covers connstr, placeholders, null_types, temporal.
fix: Introduce a small internal trait (e.g. `trait Wire { fn advance(); fn on_rows(); fn has_open_batch(); fn next_row_into<W: RowWriter>(..); fn take_info(); fn close_query(); }`) implemented by TdsClient and by a scripted fake (two adapters = real seam). Make Slot generic or hold Box<dyn Wire>. Then unit-test MARS drain, pending_error ordering, more_results with queued results, fetchall batching in pure cargo tests. Also reduces dependence on the pinned mssql-tds API surface.
verify: The facts check out. fill_pending, drain_into_buffer and release_wire in src/statement.rs all take the concrete &mut TdsClient and call block_on. The only unit tests in src/ are in connstr.rs (docs/ARCHITECTURE.md lists `cargo test --lib` as "no DB"), and I did not check the other modules for tests. The state transitions (on_wire, result_done, pending_error, queued) are therefore only covered by tests that need a live SQL Server. I could not confirm this is a should-fix, for these reasons. (1) It is a testability preference, not a defect. The goal is to pass the upstream test suite, and that suite exercises MARS drain, multiple result sets and read-ahead errors against the real server. (2) A scripted fake would encode our guesses about mssql-tds behavior, such as when has_open_batch flips and when take_info_messages returns data. The tests would then prove little about real errors. (3) The proposed trait is large and async. It would need generics or Box<dyn> through Slot, and those paths are hot, so it risks the performance goal. (4) A decode seam already exists: read_rows_into is generic over RowWriter. I found no contradiction with CONTRACT.md. Downgrade to a nit or backlog idea, because the cost is high relative to the benefit.

title: Arrow sink seam is documented but not actually deep: read_rows_into is a free fn taking two closures and a TdsClient, wired to the Python buffering state
evidence: `pub fn read_rows_into<W: RowWriter + Send>(client, sink, rows_written: impl Fn(&W)->usize, bytes_written: impl Fn(&W)->usize, max_rows, max_bytes)` — every sink must be paired with counting closures (callers pass `|b| b.rows, RowBuffer::byte_size` at L181 and L232). src/arrow.rs is a 27-line stub whose doc comment says to 'hold the connection lock' and call read_rows_into manually, while StmtState.pending is hard-typed `RowBuffer` and `fetch()` (L459) returns `Fetched{rows: RowBuffer}`. An Arrow path will have to duplicate the lock/owner/pending_error/diag/readahead choreography of fetch()+fill_pending.
fix: Define `trait RowSink: RowWriter + Send { fn rows(&self)->usize; fn byte_size(&self)->usize; }` (removes the closure params) and make the cursor module generic over sink: `Cursor::read<S: RowSink>(&mut self, wire, sink, limits) -> ReadOutcome`. fetch() becomes `fetch_with(stmt, n, readahead, make_sink)`; Python fetch and DDBCSQLFetchArrowBatch are then two ~10-line adapters over the same locked/diag/error-ordering core. Leftover rows in `pending` for an Arrow fetch must be addressed (pending is Cell-based; Arrow needs to drain it first or the sink must be selected at execute time) - decide that in the design.
verify: The code matches the finding. read_rows_into (src/statement.rs:150) takes two counting closures. Both callers (L181, L232) pass `|b| b.rows` and `RowBuffer::byte_size`. `StmtState.pending` is a concrete `RowBuffer`. src/arrow.rs is a stub that returns IM001. A `RowSink` trait (`rows()` and `byte_size()`) would remove the closure parameters. That is a small, cheap tidy-up, and the function is not part of the upstream-compatible Python surface, so nothing in CONTRACT.md blocks it. The rest of the finding overreaches. (1) The "will have to duplicate the lock/owner/pending_error/diag choreography" claim is speculation about code that doesn't exist yet. (2) docs/ARROW_PLAN.md plans a pipelined Arrow path with a bounded channel and a decode task ahead of Python. That is a different control flow from fetch()'s synchronous `pending` readahead, so a generic `fetch_with(make_sink)` may be the wrong abstraction. (3) The leftover-`pending` question matters only if Arrow and row fetches are mixed on one cursor, and the finding itself leaves that open. (4) Refactoring fetch() before the Arrow design is settled risks churn on the hot path. Upgrading the closures to a trait is optional polish, not a should-fix. Decide the design when the Arrow sink is implemented.

title: execute_command and execute_batch duplicate the entire statement preamble; ownership/diag/timeout logic is copy-pasted
evidence: execute_batch L609-625 is identical to execute_command L368-393: `conn.slot.lock(); release_wire(...); stmt.state.lock(); state.diag.clear(); state.reset_results(); let Some(client)=slot.client.as_mut() else {not_connected...}; CancelHandle::new(); *stmt.cancel.lock()=...; prepare_session(...)`. Notably execute_batch omits the `state.freed` -> SQL_INVALID_HANDLE check that execute_command has (L374), so executemany on a freed handle proceeds. Also the 'SUCCESS -> SUCCESS_WITH_INFO if diag' epilogue is repeated at L445, L693, L890, L920 and the @P{n} naming at statement.rs:323, :649, params/mod.rs:55, catalog.rs:59/81/87.
fix: Extract `fn with_exclusive_wire(stmt, |ctx: &mut ExecCtx{client, state, conn, handle, timeout}| -> SqlReturn)` that does lock, release_wire, diag clear, reset, freed check, closed-connection check, cancel handle, prepare_session once; both execute paths and catalog become closures over it. Add `fn finish(ret, &state) -> SqlReturn` for the INFO promotion and `RpcParameter::positional(i, t)` helper for @Pn.
verify: The duplication is real. execute_batch (L609-625) repeats the lock, release_wire, diag clear, reset_results, client check, CancelHandle and prepare_session preamble from execute_command (L368-393). execute_batch also lacks the `state.freed` -> SQL_INVALID_HANDLE check that execute_command has at L374, and `freed` is set by close_cursor(free=true), so executemany on a freed handle proceeds. That is a minor robustness gap, not a likely bug, because the Python layer doesn't call executemany after free. The proposed refactor is plausible but only moderately valuable. The preamble is about 15 lines, and the closure-based `with_exclusive_wire` plus an `ExecCtx` struct adds indirection around locks that borrow `slot.client` and `state`, which is a borrow-checker cost. The repeated INFO-promotion epilogue and @P{n} naming are also minor; I did not verify the cited line numbers beyond the preamble. This is not blocking and not a correctness defect in practice. At most, add the missing freed check to execute_batch now (one line) and extract a small preamble helper later. I downgrade it from should-fix to nit.

title: Command enum has an unrepresentable state papered over with unreachable!()
evidence: `enum Command { Batch(String), Rpc(String, ParamSet), RawRpc(String, Vec<RpcParameter>) }` — execute_command converts Rpc->RawRpc before use, then the second match has `Command::Rpc(..) => unreachable!("converted above")`. Also `prepare_session(.., handle: &CancelHandle)` takes a param it ignores (`let _ = handle;` L363) and `check_error(handle_type, ..)` does `let _ = handle_type;`.
fix: Make resolve_null_types a step producing Vec<RpcParameter> from ParamSet up front, so Command has only Batch and Rpc(sql, Vec<RpcParameter>); drop the unused `handle` parameter from prepare_session.
verify:
The code matches the finding. execute_command rewrites Command::Rpc into RawRpc, and the second match then has `Command::Rpc(..) => unreachable!("converted above")` (L403). prepare_session also takes `handle` and does `let _ = handle;`. Two caveats weaken it.

First, resolve_null_types needs the locked `client` to describe parameter types, so the conversion can't move "up front" before the lock. The fix would have to be a local restructure inside execute_command, such as matching straight into a Vec<RpcParameter>. The finding's suggested fix is imprecise on this point.

Second, `check_error(handle_type, ..)` is the DDBCSQLCheckError pyfunction, whose signature must match upstream. Its `let _ = handle_type` is deliberate, so it is not a defect.

What remains is a small, safe cleanup: drop the unused `handle` parameter from prepare_session, and optionally tidy the Command conversion. The `unreachable!` is internal, local and can't fire. docs/CONTRACT.md does not contradict the change, and the cleanup has no effect on behavior or performance.

title: Python-binding facade and domain logic are interleaved: ODBC argument decoding and Python-object conversion live inside the same fns that own locking
evidence: `execute()` parses params, validates marker count, writes `isStmtPrepared` list, builds diag records by locking state directly (L571-583), then py.detach(execute_command). `execute_many` (L699-737) does the Python column->SqlType loop and marker validation in the pyfunction. `more_results` (L872-929, ~55 lines) is domain logic written inline inside py.detach in the pyfunction, directly manipulating state.pending/pending_pos/columns (the same resets as StmtState::reset_results, duplicated at L877-882 apart from on_wire/result_done). Every pyfunction repeats `stmt_of(handle)?` plus 5 `#[allow(non_snake_case, unused_variables)]` ignored params (charEncoding, wcharEncoding, charCtype, encodingSettings).
fix: Pyfunctions should be <=10 lines: `let stmt = stmt_of(h)?; let args = parse(...)?; Ok(py.detach(|| stmt.execute(args)))`. Move more_results into a `StmtShared::next_result()` method and reuse StmtState::reset_results (add a parameter for what to preserve); move the marker-count validation into params (`ParamSet::check_markers`). A `Handle<'py>` newtype with FromPyObject would remove stmt_of boilerplate.
verify:
The facts check out against src/statement.rs, but this is a style refactor with no bug behind it and only some of the suggested fixes hold up.

What matches the code:
- `execute()` (L563-597) parses the params, validates the marker count, pushes a `DiagRecord` under the state lock, and writes the `isStmtPrepared` list before calling `py.detach`.
- `more_results` (L872-929) is about 55 lines of state-machine logic inline in the pyfunction.
- There are 20 `stmt_of` call sites.

What is weaker than the finding says:
- The `more_results` reset is not a duplicate of `StmtState::reset_results`. `reset_results` also clears `queued`, sets `on_wire=false` and sets `result_done=true`. `more_results` has to keep `queued` and `on_wire`, because it pops the next queued result or advances the wire. Reusing it would mean adding a parameter, which gains little for a six-line block.
- The `#[allow(non_snake_case, unused_variables)]` and the ignored params (`charEncoding` and similar) are forced by the upstream ddbc_bindings signature. The drop-in contract requires the same names and arity, and Python callers pass them by keyword. The extra parameters cannot be removed.
- Moving `more_results` into a `StmtShared::next_result()` method is reasonable for readability and unit testing. It does not change behaviour or performance.
- The `Handle<'py>` newtype only removes a one-line `stmt_of` call.

Nothing is wrong or at risk: lock ordering (slot, then state) is consistent, and `py.detach` is used correctly. A tidy-up of `more_results` and the marker check would be fine, but it is optional.

title: resolve_null_types does protocol work (run sp_describe_undeclared_parameters, parse rows) inside statement.rs, bypassing the params/null_types seam
evidence: params/null_types.rs only maps a type-name string to SqlType (69 lines), but the actual describe query, string-escaping SQL injection-style `sql.replace('\'', "''")`, row parsing (`rows.cells.chunks(ncols.max(1))`, hard-coded column indices `row.get(1)`, `row.get(3)`) and the per-connection cache (ConnShared::param_types in connection.rs) are split across statement.rs and connection.rs. Errors are swallowed: on failure it returns Vec::new() and silently leaves NVARCHAR(1) typing. The cache is cleared entirely when 512 entries are hit (`cache.clear()`).
fix: Make params::null_types a deep module: `resolve(conn_cache: &mut ParamTypeCache, wire: &mut impl Wire, sql, &mut ParamSet)` owning the describe query, row parsing, cache (LRU) and error policy. statement.rs then calls one function. Also centralise column indices as named consts.
verify: The facts are accurate. resolve_null_types (statement.rs:~284) builds the describe query, parses rows by hard-coded indices 1 and 3, and handles errors. The cache lives in connection.rs, and params/null_types.rs only maps a type-name string to SqlType. So the logic is split across three files. Several claims are overstated, though. The `replace('\'', "''")` is correct escaping for an N'...' literal, and the SQL being described is the caller's own statement, so this is not an injection risk. Swallowing the error and falling back to the default NVARCHAR typing is deliberate, matches ODBC's lenient behavior, and a failed describe is not cached. A 512-entry cache that clears itself when full is a bounded, simple policy, and LRU would be churn for a cold path. CONTRACT.md does not constrain this, because it is internal Rust code with no upstream-compat impact. The valid part is small: move the describe and parse step into params::null_types and name the two column-index constants. It is optional cleanup, not should-fix.

title: Connection attribute handling and session-state live in two places (constructor vs set_attr) and ConnShared splits one concern over five fields
evidence: Constructor loop L170-203 (SQL_ATTR_AUTOCOMMIT / TXN_ISOLATION / CURRENT_CATALOG / timeouts) re-implements the same attribute switch as set_attr L293-320 with different semantics (deferred via pending_session_sql vs immediate run_session_sql); the magic list `101 | 104 | 105 | 106 | 107 | 110 | 111 | 4 | 117 | 119 | 1207 | 1208 => Ok(())` is unnamed. ConnShared holds autocommit, implicit_txn, pending_session_sql as separate atomics/mutexes, while prepare_session in statement.rs reads and flips them (conn.take_pending_session_sql, set_implicit_transactions) - session policy lives in the statement module, not the connection.
fix: Create `SessionState` inside ConnShared with `apply_attr(attr, value) -> SessionEffect` used by both ctor and set_attr, and `fn sql_to_sync(&self) -> Option<String>` that encapsulates the IMPLICIT_TRANSACTIONS toggle currently in statement::prepare_session. Name the accepted-noop constants in consts.rs.
verify: Partly confirmed. The unnamed no-op attribute list at connection.rs L318 is real. So is the IMPLICIT_TRANSACTIONS toggle logic living in statement::prepare_session (statement.rs L334-362) instead of on ConnShared. However, the ctor/set_attr duplication is overstated. The constructor handles different attributes (access token, login timeout) and defers work because no session exists yet. It also ignores bad values where set_attr raises. Only the isolation and catalog parsing is shared, and that is already factored into isolation_sql and quote_ident. The five ConnShared fields are independent, and splitting them is deliberate for the hot paths. Nothing in CONTRACT.md is violated. The suggested SessionState/SessionEffect abstraction is more churn than the problem is worth. The cheap fixes are to name the no-op constants and move the implicit-txn SQL builder into a ConnShared method.

title: Wire-ownership protocol is split across connection.rs and statement.rs, with two sources of truth and no test seam
evidence: `Slot { client, owner: Option<(u64, Weak<StmtShared>)> }` is defined in connection.rs:~24, but its protocol (`release_wire`, `drain_into_buffer`, `fill_pending`) lives in statement.rs, and connection.rs imports back `use crate::statement::{SqlHandle, StmtShared, release_wire}` while statement.rs imports `crate::connection::{ConnShared, Slot}` (a module cycle). Ownership is recorded twice: `Slot.owner` and `StmtState.on_wire`, and they are updated by hand in 6 places (execute_command:442, more_results:915-918, release_wire:263, drain_into_buffer:248, close_cursor:520, fill_pending:192). Result state is four loose fields (`on_wire`, `result_done`, `pending_error`, `columns.is_none()`) rather than one enum. `Slot.client` is the concrete `TdsClient`, so the MARS emulation (the most intricate code in the crate) has no unit tests and needs a live SQL Server. Deletion test: removing `release_wire` pushes its complexity into execute_command, execute_batch, more_results, close_cursor and `Connection::client_op`/`close`, so it earns its keep, but it sits at the wrong seam. Design-it-twice. (A) Extract a deep `wire` module whose whole interface is `Wire::acquire(stmt_id) -> WireGuard` (derefs to `&mut TdsClient`, drains the previous owner on acquire) and `Wire::release()`. It owns `owner`, `on_wire` and drain, and `Slot` moves there. (B) Model each statement as one enum `Cursor { Idle, Streaming{result_done}, Buffered{queue}, Failed(err) }` and make `fetch` and `more_results` pull from a `ResultSource` with two adapters, `WireSource` and `BufferedSource`, which removes `install_buffered` and the duplicate paths in `fetch` and `more_results`. (A) is the cheaper first step and (B) builds on it. Put `trait Wire` (TdsClient plus a scripted fake) under (A) so the state machine can be tested without a DB. That gives two adapters, so the seam is real.
fix: Create src/wire.rs holding Slot, owner tracking, drain/release and a `Wire` trait with a TdsClient adapter and a scripted fake. statement.rs and connection.rs then depend only on wire, which breaks the cycle. Replace `on_wire`/`result_done`/`pending_error` with a single cursor-phase enum, and unit-test MARS interleavings (A executes, B executes, A fetches; commit mid-fetch; owner dropped) with the fake.
verify:
The factual claims hold. Slot is defined in connection.rs:~24, but release_wire, drain_into_buffer and fill_pending are in statement.rs (lines 170, 201, 253). connection.rs imports back from statement (`use crate::statement::{SqlHandle, StmtShared, release_wire}`), and statement.rs imports `crate::connection::{ConnShared, Slot}`. Ownership is kept in two places, `Slot.owner` and `StmtState.on_wire`, and hand-synced at lines 263, 442-443, 520-521 and 916-917. Result state is spread over `on_wire`, `result_done`, `pending_error` and `columns`. src/ has no unit tests outside connstr.rs, so the MARS code needs a live server.

The finding is still weak as a should-fix, for these reasons.
- A module cycle inside one Rust crate is harmless, and the compiler accepts it.
- The two ownership records are a consistent two-sided invariant, guarded by the single slot mutex. I found no concrete desync bug, and the finding gives none.
- The proposed `trait Wire` over TdsClient would have to mirror a wide, async-ish surface: on_rows, advance, get_metadata, close_query, has_open_batch and read_rows_into. That makes a large refactor of the riskiest code in the crate. It would not advance either project goal, which are passing upstream tests and speed. Upstream tests exercise this code against a real server.
- docs/ARCHITECTURE.md already documents the MARS design, and nothing in CONTRACT.md is contradicted either way.

What remains is a real but modest testability and cohesion concern. A cheap partial step is moving Slot and release_wire into one small module, which would also remove the cycle. That is a nit, not a blocking or should-fix item.

title: _cancel and query timeout are wired only to execute; the fetch path ignores them
evidence: ARCHITECTURE.md says `_cancel` 'cancels via CancelHandle'. `CancelHandle` is created and stored only in `execute_command` (lines 382-383, used at 398) and `execute_batch` (619-620). `fill_pending` -> `read_rows_into` -> `client.next_row_into(sink)` (lines 158-166) never receives the handle or a timeout. So `cursor.cancel()` and `SQL_ATTR_QUERY_TIMEOUT` have no effect on a `fetchall()` of a slow or blocked result (for example a lock wait mid-stream). The handle also stays in `stmt.cancel` after the statement finishes, so a stale `_cancel` is not a no-op by design.
fix: Thread an `Option<&CancelHandle>` (and the deadline) through `read_rows_into`, using `tokio::select!` on `handle.cancelled()` around `next_row_into`, or `tokio::time::timeout` for the query timeout. Clear `stmt.cancel` when the statement finishes or is reset. Add a test in tests/common_issues/test_timeouts_cancel.py that cancels or times out during fetch, not only during execute.
verify: The code matches the finding. CancelHandle and timeout_secs are passed only in execute_command (around lines 383-398) and execute_batch (around 620-653). read_rows_into (lines 148-166) calls client.next_row_into with neither, so a cancel or SQL_ATTR_QUERY_TIMEOUT cannot interrupt a blocked mid-stream fetch. Three points keep it a nit: (1) execute pre-reads the first row through fill_pending(…, 1, …) inside the cancel-aware window, so the common blocking cases (lock waits, errors before any row) are covered. Only stalls after the first row are uncovered. (2) Upstream has no public Cursor.cancel(), and docs/CONTRACT.md lists _cancel only as a SqlHandle method with no fetch-time guarantee, so upstream tests don't require this. (3) The 'stale handle' point is weak: every execute creates a fresh CancelHandle and overwrites stmt.cancel, so a stale cancel() cannot leak into the next statement. At worst it is a harmless no-op on an already-finished handle. The ARCHITECTURE.md line 'cancels via CancelHandle' slightly overpromises. The fix is real but optional: thread the handle and a deadline into the block_on in read_rows_into, and add a fetch-time cancel/timeout test.

title: fetchone allocates a new RowBuffer per row (slice_rows), contradicting the O(1)-allocation design
evidence: `fetch_one` -> `fetch(&stmt, 1, FETCHONE_READAHEAD)` -> `state.take_pending(1)`. Unless exactly one row is pending, this takes the slow branch `self.pending.slice_rows(self.ncols(), self.pending_pos, n)` (line 107). `slice_rows` (buffer.rs:130-145) builds `RowBuffer::new()` and re-copies every Utf8/Utf16/Bytes span with `out.push_span(...)` into a fresh, repeatedly growing arena. That is at least two heap allocations plus a copy per row, on the hottest DB-API call (`fetchone` loop), and buffer.rs:1-8 advertises 'O(1) allocations'. The benchmark workload `fetchone_100k_all_cols` exercises exactly this.
fix: Make the read-ahead chunk shareable and immutable: `pending: Arc<RowBuffer>` plus `pending_pos`. `fetch` returns `(Arc<RowBuffer>, start, count)` after dropping the locks, and `python::append_rows`/`extend_with_row` convert the `[start..start+count)` cell range under the GIL with no copy. `take_pending` then never copies. Only `fill_pending` mutates (via `Arc::make_mut` or a fresh buffer when the old one is exhausted).
verify: The mechanism is accurate. fetch_one calls fetch(&stmt, 1, 256), which calls take_pending(1) (statement.rs:~96-110). Except when exactly one row is left, it goes to slice_rows (decode/buffer.rs:130). slice_rows builds a fresh RowBuffer, reserves a cells Vec, and copies each Utf8/Utf16/Bytes span through push_span into a new arena that grows incrementally. That is at least 2 allocations plus a copy per fetchone row, and the header comment claims O(1) allocations. It is not handled elsewhere. The claim is also not contradicted by CONTRACT.md or upstream compatibility, since this is internal. But it only costs roughly 100-300ns per row, against a fetchone path that already pays for a Python call, a pyo3 boundary crossing, GIL detach/attach, two mutex locks, a diag clone and Python object creation. The O(1) comment is about batch fetch, which fetchmany/fetchall do honor (they take the whole buffer via mem::take). The proposed Arc<RowBuffer> redesign is disproportionate churn: it changes the lock and GIL handoff and the Fetched struct, and Arc::make_mut would still copy if the Python side holds a reference. Cheaper alternatives are to convert the single row under the lock-free pending buffer by passing (buffer, start) to extend_with_row, or to reuse a scratch RowBuffer. Worth doing only if the fetchone benchmark shows slice_rows in the profile, so I rate it a nit-level optimization, not should-fix.

title: read_rows_into is advertised as the decode seam but is a shallow, single-adapter seam; Arrow (the performance goal) is a stub
evidence: `pub fn read_rows_into<W: RowWriter + Send>(client, sink, rows_written: impl Fn(&W) -> usize, bytes_written: impl Fn(&W) -> usize, max_rows, max_bytes)`. The caller must know to pass `|b| b.rows` and `RowBuffer::byte_size` (lines 178-185, 225-232), so counting is leaked into every call site (2 call sites, same 6 arguments). The only adapter is `RowBuffer`, and `arrow.rs` is a 27-line stub whose doc comment describes the future seam: 'one adapter = hypothetical seam'. ARROW_PLAN.md promises that 'Decodes TDS rows straight into Arrow builders' is the main speed claim, and `DDBCSQLFetchArrowBatch` returns IM001, so tests/upstream/test_004_cursor_arrow.py cannot pass and the 3 arrow workloads in bench_taxi.py fail. The Arrow type mapping must also equal `decode/describe.rs`, but nothing forces the two to share one column-kind decision.
fix: Define `trait RowSink: RowWriter + Send { fn rows(&self) -> usize; fn byte_size(&self) -> usize; }` and make `read_rows_into(client, &mut impl RowSink, max_rows, max_bytes)`, which cuts the signature in half. Resolve a `ColumnKind` once per result from `ColumnMetadata` and use it in `describe.rs`, the Python path and the Arrow sink so the three cannot drift. Land the Arrow sink as the second real adapter before adding more seams. Until then, mark the Arrow rows in the benchmark as n/a so they do not look like a regression.
verify:
The code matches the finding. `read_rows_into` at src/statement.rs:150 takes two counting closures. Both call sites (lines 178 and 225) pass the same `|b| b.rows` and `RowBuffer::byte_size`. `RowBuffer` is the only adapter. src/arrow.rs is an IM001 stub, and its doc comment already describes the same call signature. The closure-passing is redundant, and a small `RowSink` trait with `rows()` and `byte_size()` would remove it.

The finding overreaches in three places, so it should not be graded should-fix.
- The Arrow stub is a known, documented gap. docs/CONTRACT.md line 52 lists `DDBCSQLFetchArrowBatch` as "stub". Unimplemented features are roadmap items, not architecture defects. The failing arrow tests and benchmark rows follow from that gap and from nothing else.
- The proposed trait is cheap, but it is a refactor with no behaviour change. It is best done when the Arrow sink lands and shows what the trait needs. Doing it now means guessing the shape from one adapter.
- I did not check the claim that the Arrow type mapping and `decode/describe.rs` could drift. It is speculative until Arrow code exists.

What is worth doing is the small trait cleanup, and marking the Arrow benchmark rows n/a. Neither is a bug or a risk to upstream compatibility.

title: Duplicated statement prologue, three copies of @Pn naming, and a re-implemented server diag record
evidence: `execute_batch` lines 609-625 repeat `execute_command` lines 368-389 nearly line for line: `conn.slot.lock()`, `release_wire`, `stmt.state.lock()`, `diag.clear()`, `reset_results()`, the `slot.client` None check, `CancelHandle::new()` plus `*stmt.cancel.lock() = ...`, and `prepare_session`. Note that `execute_command` checks `state.freed` and `execute_batch` does not, so a freed handle can run executemany. `format!("@P{}", i + 1)` -> `RpcParameter` is built in `ParamSet::into_rpc` (params/mod.rs:55), in `execute_batch` (statement.rs:649) and in `catalog::named` (catalog.rs:55). `execute_batch` hand-builds `DiagRecord::new(diag::sqlstate_for_server_error(e.number, e.class), e.number as i32, format!("{}[SQL Server]{}", diag::DRIVER_PREFIX, e.message))` (lines 663-669), duplicating the private `diag::server_record` (diag.rs:84) and the private `SERVER_SUBSOURCE` constant. `Command::Rpc` is converted to `RawRpc` and then matched again with `Command::Rpc(..) => unreachable!("converted above")` (line 403), an enum state that should be unrepresentable.
fix: Extract `fn with_statement_on_wire(stmt, f: impl FnOnce(&mut TdsClient, &mut StmtState, &CancelHandle) -> SqlReturn) -> SqlReturn` that owns the lock order, freed check, reset, cancel handle and prepare_session. Make `diag::server_record` pub and use it. Add `params::name_positional(Vec<SqlType>) -> Vec<RpcParameter>` and call it from all three places. Split `Command` into `Pending` (Batch/Rpc) and `Resolved` (Batch/RawRpc) so no unreachable arm is needed.
verify:
Confirmed in code. execute_batch (609-625) repeats execute_command's prologue (368-389). execute_command checks state.freed at line 374 and execute_batch does not, so that omission is real. The @P naming appears in params/mod.rs:55, statement.rs:649 and catalog.rs:59. execute_batch hand-builds the server DiagRecord at 663-669, while diag::server_record (diag.rs:84) is private. The unreachable!("converted above") arm for Command::Rpc is also there. Nothing in CONTRACT.md or upstream compatibility contradicts any of this, and none of it touches vendored code.

The finding is real but is a maintainability issue and should be downgraded to nit or low should-fix. Reasons:
- The freed gap is minor. Freed handles are likely rejected earlier (line 933 checks freed on another path), and the result is a missing guard, not a visible correctness failure.
- The duplication is about 10 lines plus a one-line @P format.
- The Pending/Resolved enum split and the closure-based with_statement_on_wire helper are bigger refactors than the duplication justifies.

Cheap fixes worth doing: add the freed check to execute_batch, and make diag::server_record pub and call it from execute_batch.

title: benchmarks/compare.py reuses stale results and renders failures as '-', so the port-vs-ODBC table can mislead
evidence: The docstring says 'existing files are reused for drivers not selected with --only, so the baseline only runs once'. Results carry no commit hash, dataset size, quick/full mode or date, so `rust_port.json` from a different build or a `--quick` run is compared against a full-run baseline (quick mode also drops 3 workloads and uses 3 repeats instead of 7). `timed()` returns `{"error": ...}` on warm-up failure, and compare.py does `results[n].get(w, {}).get("median_s")` then `if c else '-'`. The Arrow workloads (stub) and any regression that raises show up as a dash, indistinguishable from 'not measured'. Workloads return only a row count (`len(cur.fetchall())`), so nothing checks that both drivers returned the same rows or values. `timed` also only catches exceptions in the warm-up, so a failure in a timed repeat aborts the whole driver run.
fix: Have bench_taxi.py write `{meta: {driver, git_sha, mode, repeats, rows}, results}`. compare.py should refuse to compare results with mismatched mode or sha (or warn loudly), print `ERR` with the message for error entries, and assert equal row counts (optionally a cheap checksum such as sum of total_amount) across drivers. Wrap each timed repeat in the same try/except.
verify:
I confirmed the mechanics in benchmarks/compare.py and bench_taxi.py, but this is a dev benchmark script, so it is a nit rather than should-fix. Four points hold.
- Result files carry no metadata (sha, mode, date). Reuse of old files for drivers not in --only is documented, deliberate behaviour, so the staleness hazard is real but intended. A --quick rust_port run can be compared against a full-run baseline with no warning.
- Line 55 uses `.get(w, {}).get("median_s")`, and line 56 prints '-' for any falsy value. An `{"error": ...}` entry from `timed()` is therefore shown as '-', the same as 'not measured'.
- `timed()` wraps only the warm-up call in try/except (bench_taxi.py lines 43-46). An exception inside a timed repeat aborts the whole driver run. That is loud, not silent, so it is a minor point.
- Each result stores a `rows` count, but compare.py never checks it across drivers. A wrong-result regression would go unnoticed, although the row count is only a weak check anyway.
Nothing in docs/CONTRACT.md or the upstream-compat requirement covers these files, and the fix is cheap. The most useful parts are printing ERR for error entries, writing a mode/sha meta block, and comparing row counts. The severity is low because this is not a runtime path.

title: execute_batch reverses server error order and drains the row Vec from the front each chunk
evidence: For a failed batch row, `for e in &failed.errors { state.diag.insert(0, DiagRecord::new(...)); }` (lines 662-671) prepends each error in turn, so multiple errors end up in reverse order. `DDBCSQLCheckError` returns `diag.first()` (line 991), so the user sees the LAST error of the failing row instead of the first. Also `let chunk: Vec<Vec<SqlType>> = rows.drain(..take).collect();` (line 642) moves the whole remaining Vec down on every 2000-row chunk, so executemany of N rows costs O(N^2/2000) pointer moves (for 1M rows, 500 chunks each shifting up to 500k entries). `SQLExecuteMany` also materializes every cell as `Vec<Vec<SqlType>>` under the GIL (lines 720-732) before any send.
fix: Collect the row's errors into a Vec first and splice it at the front in order (`state.diag.splice(0..0, errors)`). Iterate with `let mut it = rows.into_iter(); loop { let chunk: Vec<_> = it.by_ref().take(EXECUTEMANY_CHUNK).collect(); if chunk.is_empty() { break } ... }`, or use `rows.chunks_mut` with `mem::take`. Longer term, convert and send one chunk at a time (keeping the GIL release per chunk) to bound memory.
verify: Confirmed in src/statement.rs. The loop at lines 662-671 does `diag.insert(0, …)` per error, so multiple errors on a failed row end up reversed and `diag.first()` (line 991) returns the last one. A row usually has one error, because 3621 normally arrives as an info message, so the impact is rare. `rows.drain(..take)` (line 642) is quadratic in chunk count, but it comes to about 3 GB of memmove for 1M rows, a few hundred ms, which is minor next to per-cell conversion under the GIL. The eager materialisation is a design choice, since the null-type probe and `batch::normalize` need all rows. The error-order fix is trivial; the drain change is optional.

title: PYTHON_LAYER_CHANGES.md says every edit is marked RUST-PORT, but only one marker exists
evidence: Doc: "every deliberate edit is marked `RUST-PORT` in the source and listed here". `grep -rn RUST-PORT python` returns a single hit, python/mssql_python/odbc_provider.py:158. The #581 edits listed in the table (exceptions.py, helpers.py `_native_error_from_diag_records`, connection.py `_raise_connection_error`, async_query/exception_translator.py, _server_sqlstate.py) carry no marker, so they cannot be found by grep when rebasing on upstream.

The #581 edits carry only incidental "(#581)" comments in exceptions.py and _server_sqlstate.py. The doc also has a duplicated intro paragraph, and its table is the real index of the edits. title: PYTHON_LAYER_CHANGES.md is two documents concatenated
evidence: The file opens with "# Python layer changes ... vendored from microsoft/mssql-python", then at line 13 repeats a second intro: "Edits to `python/mssql_python` relative to upstream mssql-python (commit in `tests/upstream/UPSTREAM_COMMIT`). Keep them minimal". The 'Core bindings' section (RUST-PORT edits) and the '#581' section (which says it is an upstream issue fix, not a port edit) are mixed under one rule.

verify: Confirmed. docs/PYTHON_LAYER_CHANGES.md has an intro at lines 1-5 ("vendored from microsoft/mssql-python ... every deliberate edit is marked RUST-PORT"). Lines 13-14 then repeat a second intro ("Edits to python/mssql_python relative to upstream ... Keep them minimal; each section says why."), and it sits after the Core bindings section instead of before it. It is a stray duplicate, probably left over from a merge.
