Only the duplicate intro paragraph is a real defect. Splitting into two categories is optional polish. Severity is nit.

title: Entra/`Authentication=` and `token_factory` silently ignored: falls back to password login instead of failing cleanly
evidence: CONTRACT.md lists `token_factory`/Entra as TODO. connection.rs `new` has `#[allow(unused_variables)]` and never reads `token_factory`. `build_context` ignores the `authentication` key ("Unknown keys are ignored") and ends with `else { ctx.tds_authentication_method = TdsAuthenticationMethod::Password; }`. A string with `Authentication=ActiveDirectoryPassword` or a `token_provider` therefore attempts SQL login with the AAD UID/PWD and returns a misleading 18456, not the 'stubs fail cleanly' behaviour ARCHITECTURE.md promises.
fix: In `build_context`, when `authentication` is set to anything other than `SqlPassword`, return `Err("... Authentication=<x> not implemented in Rust port")`, mapped to an IM001-style `SQLSTATE:IM001:NATIVE:0:` RuntimeError. Do the same when `token_factory.is_some()`. Add a test.
verify:
The finding is mostly wrong. The `Authentication=` half is already handled: the vendored Python layer (connection.py, around lines 659-775) resolves `Authentication=ActiveDirectory*`. It strips the key from the connection string and passes the token through `attrs_before`, which reaches `build_context` as `access_token`. The AccessToken branch at connstr.rs:158 takes it from there. The Python layer also fails closed with InterfaceError if no token can be obtained. Rust therefore never sees `Authentication=ActiveDirectory*` in normal use, and adding a rejection in `build_context` would be dead code. It could also break a legitimate `Authentication=SqlPassword` string.

A small real gap remains for the `token_factory` path. The Python layer sets `token_factory` for pooled MSI and `acct:`-keyed interactive or device-code connections, and in that case may leave `attrs_before` without a token. connection.rs:155 never reads `token_factory`, so Rust falls through to Password login with the Authentication key stripped and no UID/PWD. It fails with a login error rather than connecting as the wrong identity, so this is a missing feature, not silent misbehaviour. CONTRACT.md already lists it as TODO (line 24), and connection.rs:197 carries a TODO comment.

The cheap improvement is to return IM001 when `token_factory.is_some()` and `access_token.is_none()`. That is a nit, not should-fix.

title: Process-aborting panics remain on paths the architecture says never panic
evidence: `.build().expect("failed to build tokio runtime")` inside `OnceLock::get_or_init`, called from every `block_on`. A thread/resource limit (EAGAIN on thread spawn) panics. A PyO3 panic becomes `pyo3_runtime.PanicException` (a BaseException), which bypasses the Python layer's `except Exception` handling. Likewise `src/params/batch.rs:129,160,183,202-217` use `.unwrap()` that depend on the preceding `all(...)` guard staying in sync, and `statement.rs:403` / `py_types.rs:511,593,609` use `unreachable!`.
fix: Make `runtime()` return `Result` (or lazily record an init error) and have `block_on` callers map it to a `DiagRecord` `HY000`/`08001`. Replace the `unwrap`s in `batch.rs` with `let Some(..) = .. else { return false }` fallbacks. The `unreachable!`s can stay if the type system cannot encode them, but note that.
verify: The runtime.rs:25 `.expect()` is real, but only for a rare failure. It fires only if tokio cannot spawn worker threads, for example under an EAGAIN thread limit. A PyO3 panic would then surface as PanicException, a BaseException, instead of a DiagRecord. docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:64 says "never panic", but that line is about the ODBC-style return path. Fixing this means changing `runtime()` and every `block_on` caller, which is a lot of churn for an environment-exhaustion case. The process would be unusable in that state anyway. The batch.rs unwraps (lines 129, 160) sit directly after the `all(...)` or `any` guard over the same `values` set and the same column, so they cannot fail as written. They are a maintenance hazard only, and the `let Some` refactor is optional. The `unreachable!`s were not examined. The finding does not hold up as should-fix. At most, a cheap tidy-up is to replace the `.expect` with a clearer message or a fallible `runtime()` if one is ever needed.

title: Python exceptions raised from Rust for errors that the architecture says are reported via diag records
evidence: ARCHITECTURE.md: "Errors are not raised from Rust: they are stored as `DiagRecord`s". But `execute` does `build_rpc_params(...)?` and `execute_many` does `column.get_item(row)?` and `py_to_sql_type(&value).map_err(|e| crate::params::conversion_error(&e))?`, raising ValueError/TypeError. `conversion_error` picks the exception class by substring-matching the message: `lower.contains("precision")`, `lower.contains("range") || lower.contains("overflow")`, else TypeError. A ragged `columnwise_params` column (shorter than `paramSetSize`) raises a bare IndexError.
fix: Have `mssql-tds`/`py_types.rs` return a typed enum (OutOfRange, Precision, Unsupported) and match on it instead of on text. Document in ARCHITECTURE.md that parameter-conversion failures are raised deliberately for upstream parity. Validate the column length against `paramSetSize` and return `SQL_ERROR` with `07002`/`HY000`.
verify: The code matches the finding. execute and execute_many raise PyErr through `?`, and conversion_error picks ValueError or TypeError by substring-matching the message (src/params/mod.rs:93). The severity is overstated for three reasons. (1) The raise is deliberate, and the doc comment says "like the C++ binding". Upstream ddbc_bindings raises ValueError and TypeError for out-of-range and unsupported parameters, and upstream tests expect that. ARCHITECTURE.md's "errors are not raised" covers execution and diagnostic errors, and the same docs already carve out exceptions (connection errors raise RuntimeError). So this is a doc gap, not a contract violation, and moving these errors to diag records would break upstream parity. (2) The ragged IndexError is practically unreachable. The upstream Python layer builds columnwise_params with exactly paramSetSize entries per column, so the bare IndexError only occurs under misuse. A length check is cheap, but it is hardening, not a bug. (3) Substring matching is fragile, but the message source is the pinned mssql-tds crate, which we do not own, so a typed enum would mean changing the vendored dependency. What is worth doing is to add a one-line note to ARCHITECTURE.md that parameter-conversion errors are raised for upstream parity, and optionally to add a length check in execute_many.

title: Numeric ODBC attribute ids hard-coded in set_attr instead of named constants
evidence: `101 | 104 | 105 | 106 | 107 | 110 | 111 | 4 | 117 | 119 | 1207 | 1208 => Ok(()),` while the neighbouring arms use `SQL_ATTR_*` from consts.rs, and ARCHITECTURE.md gives consts.rs ownership of ODBC constants shared with constants.py. This is a Mysterious-Name smell; the silently accepted attributes (e.g. 1207/1208 = SQL_COPT_SS_*) are not auditable.

This is a cosmetic one-line change. The doc half is mostly handled already. title: GIL held while waiting on connection and statement mutexes
evidence: `get_info` runs `conn.slot.lock()` with the GIL attached. The slot is held for the full duration of any execute, fetch or drain on another thread (those run `block_on` inside `py.detach`). The same pattern appears in statement.rs with `stmt.state.lock()` taken under the GIL: lines 577 (`execute` arg-count error path), 740 (`row_count`), 747 (`num_result_cols`), 760 (`describe_col`), 933 and 937 (`reset_stmt`), 968 (`get_all_diag_records`), 991 (`check_error`). `state` is also held by another thread's `drain_into_buffer`, which can read an entire result set. ARCHITECTURE.md says locks are "taken only with the GIL released"; these sites contradict it. There is no deadlock, because the holder drops its locks before re-attaching, but one thread's query freezes every Python thread.
fix: Wrap each of these lock acquisitions in `py.detach(|| ...)`. Alternatively, mirror `rowcount`, `ncols`, `columns` and `diag` into a small separate `Mutex` or atomics that is never held across I/O. For `get_info`, cache `server_version`, `database` and `server_name` in `ConnShared` at connect time.
verify: Confirmed in the code. src/getinfo.rs:24 takes `conn.slot.lock()` with the GIL attached. The `stmt.state.lock()` calls in statement.rs at 577, 740, 747, 760, 933, 937, 968 and 991 are also under the GIL, which I confirmed from the surrounding lines. docs/ARCHITECTURE.md lines 71-72 say both locks are "taken only with the GIL released", so these sites contradict the stated model. The holder paths (the lock sites at statement.rs:369, 460 and 610) run network I/O while holding slot and state, so a blocked waiter would freeze all Python threads. I found no deadlock, because the holder does not need the GIL while it holds the lock. I did not read the holder paths' detach structure in detail. Nothing in docs/CONTRACT.md or upstream compatibility blocks a fix; the fix is local and does not change the Python API. The practical impact is small. Contention needs two threads using the same connection or statement at once, which DB-API threadsafety=1 does not permit. `cancel` uses a separate lock, so the common cross-thread cancel case is not affected. The finding is real, but the likely fix is correcting the ARCHITECTURE.md wording and optionally caching the `get_info` fields at connect time, not a blocking change. I graded it nit rather than should-fix.

title: Setup, describe, commit/rollback/close and drain paths have no cancel or timeout and hold the connection mutex; Ctrl-C is never delivered
evidence: `prepare_session(conn, client, timeout, &handle)` ends with `let _ = handle;`, so the session SQL (`SET IMPLICIT_TRANSACTIONS`, `USE`, isolation) runs without the cancel handle. `resolve_null_types` uses `client.execute(query, ())` with no options. `client_op`/`run_session_sql` (connection.rs:129-137) call commit, rollback and `client.execute(sql, ())` with `None, None`. `release_wire` and `close()` call `close_query()` with no handle. All of these run under `slot.lock()` inside `py.detach(block_on(..))`, and `block_on` never polls Python signals. A hung server therefore wedges every thread that touches the connection, `_cancel()` (which only touches the execute-time handle) has no effect, and KeyboardInterrupt cannot interrupt it. `connection_timeout` is stored (connection.rs:36, 309) but never applied.
fix: Pass `ExecuteOptions::new().timeout_secs(..).cancel(&handle)` to the setup, describe and session calls. Apply `connection_timeout` to commit, rollback and close. Make the detached waits interruptible: run `block_on` in a loop with a short `tokio::time::timeout` and check `Python::check_signals()` between slices, cancelling the active handle on interrupt.
verify: The code facts mostly check out. `prepare_session` ends with `let _ = handle;`. `resolve_null_types` and `run_session_sql` call `client.execute` with no timeout and no cancel. `release_wire` calls `close_query()` with no handle. `block_on` (src/runtime.rs) never polls Python signals. The finding overstates this in three ways. (1) The `prepare_session` SQL does get `.timeout_secs(timeout)`, so it is not "no timeout". It only lacks the cancel handle. (2) The main execute path also runs `block_on` with no `check_signals`. So Ctrl-C is already not delivered during ordinary queries, and the setup/commit/close paths are not a special gap. ODBC's `SQLExecute` behaves the same way, so this matches upstream. (3) `connection_timeout` is the ODBC login timeout (`SQL_ATTR_LOGIN_TIMEOUT`). Applying it to commit, rollback or close would be wrong and would break upstream compatibility. A real hang on a dead server is possible, since the default `query_timeout` is 0, which means unlimited. It is the same hang the ODBC driver has, and it is a robustness improvement, not a correctness bug. The signal-polling `block_on` loop is a worthwhile change, but it should be a separate design item. I'm downgrading from should-fix to nit and dropping the `connection_timeout` part of the fix.

title: Connection is a non-frozen pyclass with &mut self close(), so concurrent commit/close raises 'Already borrowed'
evidence: `#[pyclass(name = "Connection", ...)] pub struct Connection { shared, closed: bool, pool_key }` with `fn close(&mut self, ...)`, while `commit`, `rollback`, `set_attr`, `get_info` and `client_op` take `&self` and keep the PyO3 shared borrow alive across `py.detach` and network I/O. If thread A is inside `commit()` and thread B calls `close()` (or the reverse), PyO3 raises `RuntimeError: Already borrowed` instead of waiting or closing cleanly. `closed` and `pool_key` are plain fields, so they cannot be shared safely any other way.
fix: Mark the class `frozen` and move `closed` to an `AtomicBool` and `pool_key` to `Mutex<Option<String>>`, or put them inside `ConnShared`. Make `close(&self)` use `closed.swap(true)`. Then borrow conflicts cannot occur and the close/commit race is decided by the slot mutex.
verify: The code matches the finding. `Connection` is a plain `#[pyclass]` with `closed: bool` and `pool_key: Option<String>`. `close(&mut self)` holds an exclusive PyO3 borrow across `py.detach` and the `shared.slot.lock()` wait. `commit`, `rollback`, `set_attr`, `get_info` and `client_op` hold shared borrows across network I/O. Cross-thread overlap of `close` with any of those therefore gives PyO3's "Already borrowed" RuntimeError. Nothing in docs/CONTRACT.md or the upstream-compat constraints requires this behaviour. The bad outcome is only a spurious RuntimeError, not memory unsafety or a deadlock. The trigger is narrow: closing a connection from another thread while a commit or rollback is in flight on that same connection. Cursor and statement work goes through `SqlHandle`/`StmtShared` and does not borrow `Connection`, so ordinary multi-threaded cursor use is unaffected. Upstream's C++ binding would block on its own mutex instead of erroring, so the fix is a cheap fidelity improvement (an AtomicBool, `Mutex<Option<String>>` and a frozen class), but I rate it a nit rather than should-fix.

title: A failed rollback does not stop the session from being returned to the pool
evidence: `close()` runs `let _ = block_on(client.rollback_transaction(None, None));` and then `crate::pooling::checkin(key, client)`. `checkin` only rejects clients with `is_connection_dead()` or `has_open_batch()`. If the rollback returned an error (timeout, server error, cancel), the session may still have an open transaction and holds locks while idle in `IDLE`. Reset happens only on the next checkout. Separately, `checkout` only evicts entries of the same key, so idle clients for keys never requested again are never expired, and sockets stay open until `close_pooling`.
fix: Capture the rollback result and, on error, call `client.mark_connection_dead()` or `close_connection()` instead of checking the client in. Add a sweep of expired entries in `checkin` (iterate `IDLE` and drop entries older than the idle timeout).
verify:
The code matches the finding. In src/connection.rs close(), the rollback result is discarded with `let _ =`, and the client then goes to `pooling::checkin` (src/pooling.rs:50). `checkin` rejects only clients where `is_connection_dead()` or `has_open_batch()` is true. A rollback that fails for a non-fatal reason (server error or timeout) could leave the transaction open. A client in that state would sit idle in the pool holding locks until the next checkout. `checkout` calls `prepare_reset_connection(false)`, which resets the session and normally rolls back the transaction, but only when that key is requested again. The second claim is also accurate: `checkout` only evicts entries for its own key, and `checkin` never sweeps, so idle sockets for keys that are never requested again stay open until `close_pooling`.

Why this is only a nit:
- Most rollback failures are I/O errors, which would already mark the connection dead, so `checkin` would reject it.
- The failure window is narrow, and the session reset is a safety net on reuse.
- The idle-socket leak is bounded by `max_size` per key and affects only resource use, not correctness.
- Nothing in docs/CONTRACT.md is violated, but the upstream C++ code may behave the same way.

A cheap fix is to re-check `client.has_active_transaction()` after the rollback and close the client instead of checking it in. The sweep in `checkin` is optional.

title: SA password passed on the sqlcmd command line
evidence: `podman exec mssql-rs /opt/mssql-tools18/bin/sqlcmd -C -S localhost -U sa -P "$MSSQL_SA_PASSWORD" -b -Q "IF DB_ID('$_db') IS NULL CREATE DATABASE [$_db]"` exposes the password in `ps` output and `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` of every local user for the life of the call. `$_db` is sanitised with `tr -c 'A-Za-z0-9_\n' '_'`, so it is not injectable.
fix: Pass it through the environment: `podman exec -e SQLCMDPASSWORD="$MSSQL_SA_PASSWORD" ...` and drop `-P`.
verify: The code at scripts/env.sh line 12 matches the finding: `-P "$MSSQL_SA_PASSWORD"` goes on the sqlcmd command line. Nothing in the docs or upstream compatibility conflicts with changing it. The risk is low, because this is a local throwaway dev container, the exposure lasts well under a second, and the machine is single-user. Treat it as a nit. The proposed fix is incomplete: `podman exec -e SQLCMDPASSWORD="$val"` still puts the value in podman's argv on the host. Use `export SQLCMDPASSWORD=...` and then `podman exec -e SQLCMDPASSWORD`, which forwards the value without printing it.

title: Write-only stubs presented as features: DECIMAL_SEPARATOR and logging LEVEL
evidence: `static DECIMAL_SEPARATOR: Mutex<String>` is only written in `set_decimal_separator` (`if let Ok(mut s) = DECIMAL_SEPARATOR.lock() { *s = separator; }`) and never read. In logging.rs, `pub fn level() -> i32 { LEVEL.load(...) }` has no caller (grep for `logging::level` finds nothing). The comments say 'stored for parity, unused by the native decoder' and 'nothing native logs yet, so the level is stored'. This is speculative state and speculative API, and it carries a `TODO(logging)`.
fix: Make `DDBCSetDecimalSeparator` and `update_log_level` plain no-ops with a one-line doc ('accepted for API compatibility; the native decoder does not format decimals as text'). Remove the statics, the `Mutex`/`lock()` poison handling and `logging::level()`. Re-add them when a reader exists.
verify: The dead state is confirmed. `DECIMAL_SEPARATOR` (src/lib.rs:31) is only written, at line 62. `logging::level()` has no caller; `update_log_level` is registered at lib.rs:118. CONTRACT.md:63 already lists `DDBCSetDecimalSeparator` as "stored; not needed by native decode", so a no-op would still match the contract. Nothing about upstream compatibility requires the storage, because only the Python-visible function names matter. It is a nit, not should-fix. The cost is a few lines, a likely dead_code warning on `level()`, and a comment that is honest about the state. `logging.rs` also carries an explicit TODO to route tracing events to the Python logger, which makes the stored level a deliberate placeholder. The decimal separator is also a possible behaviour gap: if any path formats decimals as text, the setting would silently do nothing. Removing the static would hide that gap rather than fix it. The cleanup is optional, low-churn, and best folded into any pass that touches these files.

title: Dummy parameters kept alive with `let _ =` instead of underscore-prefixed names
evidence: `prepare_session(.., handle: &CancelHandle)` ends with `let _ = handle; Ok(())`, and both call sites (lines 386 and 622) build and pass `&handle` for nothing. `fetch_scroll` has `let _ = FetchOffset;` (862) and `check_error` has `let _ = handle_type;` (978). Elsewhere the same job is done with `#[allow(unused_variables)]` on `execute`, `fetch_one`, `Connection::new` and others. There are three different idioms for one problem.

For the pyfunction signatures that must keep ODBC names, use one idiom: `_`-prefixed parameters with `#[pyo3(name=..)]` where pyo3 allows it, or a single `#[allow(unused_variables)]` per function. Delete the `let _ = x;` lines.
verify: Confirmed in code. prepare_session (statement.rs:334-364) takes `handle: &CancelHandle` that it never uses, ending with `let _ = handle;`, and callers at 386 and 622 pass `&handle` for nothing. `let _ = FetchOffset;` (862) and `let _ = handle_type;` (978) also exist alongside several `#[allow(unused_variables)]` attributes, so the idioms are mixed. Only the prepare_session case is a clear cleanup: dropping the dead internal parameter is safe and does not affect the upstream-compatible API. The pyfunction ones are less clear. Their ODBC-style names probably must stay as they are for upstream compatibility, and the fix suggested for them (`_`-prefixed names with `#[pyo3(name=..)]`) would not apply to positional arguments, so I could not confirm it. The harm is cosmetic: no behaviour change, no bug. It is a nit, not should-fix.

title: Needless temp binding in text_param
evidence:
`let sql_type = match value { ... };
    sql_type` followed by a redundant `(s.encode_utf16().count().max(1)).min(4000)` with extra parentheses.
fix: Return the `match` expression directly and use `.clamp(1, 4000)`: `s.encode_utf16().count().clamp(1, 4000) as u16`.

title: Unreachable enum variant forces `unreachable!` in execute_command
evidence: `Command::Rpc(sql, mut params)` is converted to `RawRpc` before the match that runs it, so the second match needs `Command::Rpc(..) => unreachable!("converted above")`. The code relies on a comment ("converted above") to stay correct, and `resolve_null_types` also gets the `ParamSet` only through this path.

The suggested fix does not work as written. `resolve_null_types` needs the locked `client` and `conn`, and may do a server round trip. That only happens inside `execute_command`, after the locks are taken and `prepare_session` has run, so the callers (lines 594, 1012, 1023) cannot resolve Rpc into `Vec<RpcParameter>` earlier. A cleaner design would split a caller-facing enum from an executable one, or resolve inside a helper that returns `RawRpc`. That is a small refactor of one private enum and gives no behaviour change. This is a minor tidy-up and not a should-fix.

title: Magic attribute numbers in set_attr with no names or reasons
evidence: `// Accepted for compatibility; no TDS-level effect.\n 101 | 104 | 105 | 106 | 107 | 110 | 111 | 4 | 117 | 119 | 1207 | 1208 => Ok(()),`. The comment restates 'accepted' but not which ODBC attributes these are or why accepting them silently is right. Neighbouring arms use named consts from consts.rs. The same applies to getinfo.rs, where `30 | 35 | 32 | 34 => Info::Int(128)` is only explained by `SQL_MAX_*_NAME_LEN`.

In getinfo.rs the `30 | 35 | 32 | 34 => Info::Int(128)` arm already carries a `SQL_MAX_*_NAME_LEN` comment, and the whole file uses bare numbers with trailing comments. That part is a weak point. title: Over-defensive ignored errors with no explanation (let _ = ... and unwrap_or defaults)
evidence: `let _ = block_on(client.rollback_transaction(None, None));` and `let _ = block_on(client.close_connection());` in `close`, and `let _ = block_on(client.close_query());` / `let _ = client.take_info_messages();` at statement.rs:267-268, 301-303, 686-691. Separately, `value.extract::<i64>().unwrap_or(1) != 0` for SQL_ATTR_AUTOCOMMIT (173) and `unwrap_or(0)` for the connection timeout silently turn a bad type into a default, while `set_attr` for the same attribute raises 'Invalid attribute value'. Two behaviours for the same input.
fix: Add one WHY comment where errors are intentionally dropped, e.g. 'best effort on close: the socket may already be dead, and the error would mask the original failure'. Where it is not that case, propagate the error. Make the connect-time `attrs_before` path reject malformed autocommit/timeout values the way `set_attr` does, or comment why it must not.
verify: The code matches the finding. `close` at connection.rs:238 and 245 uses `let _ = block_on(...)`, and lines 173 and 181 use `unwrap_or(1)` and `unwrap_or(0)`. The finding is overstated, so I rate it nit rather than should-fix. (1) Ignoring errors on close and rollback is the standard best-effort teardown. Propagating them would break upstream-compatible `close()` semantics and could mask the original failure. The only gap is a one-line WHY comment, which is cosmetic. (2) The claimed inconsistency with `set_attr` is real: it raises 'Invalid attribute value' (lines 295-308), while the connect-time path defaults. But the whole `attrs_before` loop is deliberately lenient. It skips non-int keys, uses `.ok()` for login timeout and isolation, uses `if let Ok` for catalog, and ignores unknown keys with `_ => {}`. Upstream passes typed ints here, so malformed values are not a realistic input. Making only autocommit and timeout strict would add inconsistency, and docs/CONTRACT.md has no requirement either way. The statement.rs sites (267-268, 301-303, 686-691) are also best-effort cleanup and need no change. A single comment is worth adding, but no behaviour change is.

title: Redundant comprehension in load_taxi.py

The line above it (`columns = table.column_names`) exists only for this use. The 3M-row and 100k loads also repeat the same cursor/DDL/bulkcopy sequence inside the for loop with the comment `# The Arrow bulk-copy writer does not convert float64 into DECIMAL.`, which says what but not which upstream behaviour or bug.
fix: Use `mappings = list(enumerate(table.column_names))` and drop the `columns` variable. Extend the comment to name the upstream bulkcopy_arrow limitation (and link the issue in docs/UPSTREAM_BUGS_FOUND.md if one exists).

The comment half of the finding is wrong. The cast and its comment ("The Arrow bulk-copy writer does not convert float64 into DECIMAL.") appear once, before the load loop, not inside it. title: Duplicated workload bodies and broad except in bench_taxi.py
evidence: `timed()` wraps the warm-up in `except Exception as exc:  # a driver that lacks a feature still reports the rest` and returns a truncated error string `[:200]`, so a real regression in the Rust port (for example a crash in `fetchone_100k`) shows up as an 'error' cell in compare.py, with no non-zero exit. The 'quick' mode also drops workloads by name via `workloads.pop(...)` in two places. `compare.py` then silently prints '-' for missing results.
fix: Keep the catch, but have `bench_taxi.py` exit non-zero (or have compare.py print the error text) when the driver under test is `rust_port` and any workload errors. Keep the comment's WHY and add that it applies only to third-party drivers (fastmssql). Move the quick-mode exclusion into a named set so both runners share it.
verify:
The mechanism is confirmed, but the finding overstates it and is a benchmark-hygiene nit, not a comment-quality issue. In `benchmarks/bench_taxi.py`, `timed()` catches `Exception` on the warm-up only and returns a truncated `[:200]` error dict. `compare.py` reads only `median_s`, so an errored workload prints '-' and the error text is never shown. `subprocess.run(check=True)` only catches a crash of the whole runner, not a per-workload error. The catch is deliberate, because upstream ODBC has no Arrow API and the `mssql_python` runner is shared. The comment states its WHY accurately, so it is not slop. Three parts of the finding don't hold:
- The title's "duplicated workload bodies" is not supported. The two runners hold different workloads, since fastmssql has no executemany or Arrow.
- A Rust panic would not be hidden. PyO3's `PanicException` derives from `BaseException`, so `except Exception` does not catch it and the run aborts.
- Only a Python-level exception raised by the port, for example a `DatabaseError`, would show up as a silent '-'.

The quick-mode `pop` lists differ per driver because each runner has different workloads, so a shared named set would be churn. The one useful fix is small: have `compare.py` print the `error` text, or warn when a `rust_port` cell has an error instead of a result.

title: fetchone/partial fetch allocates a fresh RowBuffer (2 Vecs) per call via slice_rows
evidence: take_pending: `let out = self.pending.slice_rows(self.ncols(), self.pending_pos, n);` -> slice_rows does `let mut out = RowBuffer::new(); out.cells.reserve(..)` and `out.push_span(..)` per string cell with no arena reserve. With FETCHONE_READAHEAD=256 every fetchone() (fetch(&stmt,1,..)) copies one row's cells+arena into new Vecs; fetchmany(n) and fetchall's 8192-row batches also re-copy whenever pending > n. Only the exact-drain case (`pending_pos==0 && n==available`) is zero-copy.
fix: Don't copy: return (buffer ref, row range) and convert straight from `self.pending` under the lock-free hand-off, or keep pending in an Arc/take it and carry `pending_pos` into Fetched so python::append_rows/extend_with_row read the sub-range `cells[pos*ncols..]`. At minimum reserve `out.arena` (sum of span lens) in slice_rows so it is one allocation.
verify: Confirmed in code: take_pending only moves the buffer on the exact-drain case. Otherwise slice_rows builds a new RowBuffer, with cells reserved but no arena reserve (push_span grows it incrementally). So fetchone (readahead 256) allocates 1-2 small Vecs and copies one row per call, and fetchmany(n) copies whenever pending > n. The arena-reserve suggestion is valid and trivial. The cost is about 2 small allocations and a memcpy per fetchone, which is dwarfed by creating Python row objects and the per-call GIL, lock and detach overhead. It does not affect the bulk fetchall/Arrow path that the speed goals target. The proposed refactor (carrying pending_pos into Fetched, or Arc-sharing the buffer) touches the hand-off design for little gain. Neither CONTRACT.md nor ARCHITECTURE.md prohibits the copy. Valid but low-impact, so a nit: reserve the arena in slice_rows (sum of span lens) and skip the larger redesign unless fetchone benchmarks show it matters.

title: Unused dependencies and an unused pyo3 feature in Cargo.toml
evidence: `once_cell = "1"`, `chrono = "0.4"`, `bigdecimal = "0.4"`, `thiserror = "2"` have zero references in src/ (grep for `once_cell`, `chrono`, `BigDecimal`, `thiserror` returns nothing; statics use std OnceLock / PyOnceLock). pyo3 feature `"chrono"` is also unused: dates are built with PyDate/PyDateTime::new, no chrono conversions. tokio features `net`, `time`, `sync`, `macros` are not used by our code (only `tokio::runtime::{Builder, Runtime}` in runtime.rs).
fix: Remove once_cell, chrono, bigdecimal, thiserror and the pyo3 `chrono` feature; trim tokio to what `enable_all()` needs (verify with `cargo +nightly udeps` or cargo-machete, keep net/time only if mssql-tds does not already enable them). Shrinks compile time and LTO=fat link time.
verify: Confirmed: once_cell, chrono, bigdecimal and thiserror have no references anywhere in the .rs files (src/ and elsewhere). The pyo3 "chrono" feature is also unused, and the only tokio use is tokio::runtime::{Builder, Runtime} in src/runtime.rs. Nothing in docs/CONTRACT.md or upstream compatibility requires them. Two parts of the finding are weak. (1) The tokio trim is partly wrong: runtime.rs calls enable_all(), and the io and time drivers only exist if tokio's `net` and `time` features are on. Dropping them could leave the runtime without drivers unless mssql-tds happens to enable them, so keep `net` and `time`. Only `sync` and `macros` are plausibly removable. (2) The compile-time and LTO savings are probably small. mssql-tds very likely pulls in chrono, bigdecimal, thiserror and tokio itself, so those crates still get built. The real gain is lighter manifest hygiene and one fewer pyo3 chrono glue module. Removing the four direct deps is safe and worth a quick tidy, but it does not justify should-fix.

title: Per-cell Python call overhead for Decimal, money, UUID, datetimeoffset
evidence: uuid(): `let kwargs = PyDict::new(py); kwargs.set_item("bytes", PyBytes::new(py, value.as_bytes()))?; cls.call((), Some(&kwargs))` allocates a dict + bytes + runs UUID.__init__ per cell (own TODO(perf) admits it). numeric.rs `decimal_from_str` does `cls.call1((text,))` (str alloc + Decimal parse) per cell; money() also does `format!` (heap String) per cell. temporal.rs datetimeoffset(): `PyDelta::new` + `PyTzInfo::fixed_offset` created for every cell although offsets repeat.
fix: UUID: `object.__new__(UUID)` then set `int` via PyLong_FromUnsignedNativeBytes/_PyLong_FromByteArray (or `UUID(int=...)` positional-free via a cached `functools.partial`), as the TODO says. Decimal: build via `Decimal.__new__` from a tuple is no faster; instead cache per-column scale and use `Decimal(int).scaleb(-scale)` or at least write money into a stack buffer (like DECIMAL_STR_LEN) instead of `format!`. datetimeoffset: cache tzinfo objects per offset_minutes in a small HashMap/array for the duration of append_rows.
verify: The code matches the finding in part. uuid() builds a kwargs dict plus a bytes object and calls UUID.__init__ for every cell, and the TODO(perf) comment in binary.rs says so. datetimeoffset() creates a new PyDelta and fixed-offset tzinfo for every cell (temporal.rs:67-68), and offsets repeat heavily. money() calls format! to allocate a String per cell. The finding is overstated in three ways. First, it is a known micro-optimization, not a correctness bug, and nothing in CONTRACT.md or upstream compatibility forbids it. Second, the Decimal claim is mostly wrong: decimal() already formats into a stack buffer (DECIMAL_STR_LEN), so only money() allocates, and the `Decimal(int).scaleb(-scale)` suggestion would be slower than the current string parse. Third, `object.__new__(UUID)` plus setting `int` is fiddly. UUID is immutable and defines __slots__, so the attribute has to be set through object.__setattr__ (and is_safe also has to be set), which makes the fix riskier than it sounds. The tzinfo cache and a stack buffer for money are cheap, safe wins. The rest is optional tuning. Grade: nit, with the tzinfo cache as the only item worth doing.

title: Logging bridge is write-only: level stored, never read
evidence: `pub fn level() -> i32 { LEVEL.load(Ordering::Relaxed) }` has no callers (grep `logging::level|level()` in src returns nothing); `update_log_level` only stores into LEVEL. The module is a stub with a TODO.
fix: Either wire it up (gate tracing forwarding on `level()`) or delete `level()` and keep `update_log_level` as a documented no-op like `set_odbc_provider`, to avoid pub dead API.

title: DDBCSetDecimalSeparator stores into a Mutex<String> that nothing reads
evidence: `static DECIMAL_SEPARATOR: Mutex<String> = Mutex::new(String::new());` is only written in `set_decimal_separator` (`*s = separator;`); the comment says 'unused by the native decoder'. It also uses std Mutex while the rest of the crate uses parking_lot, silently swallowing poison with `if let Ok`.

verify: Confirmed. In src/lib.rs, DECIMAL_SEPARATOR (line 31) is only written, in set_decimal_separator (lines 58-65), and grep finds no reader anywhere in src. The code comment says "unused by the native decoder", and CONTRACT.md line 63 says "stored; not needed by native decode". The Python layer calls it only to forward settings.decimal_separator. The finding stands, but it is cosmetic: the cost is one tiny static and a rarely called setter, and CONTRACT.md documents the storing, so a fix would also need a CONTRACT.md edit. title: Unused import, dead parameter and dead const in statement/consts
evidence: `ResultSet` is imported (`use mssql_tds::connection::tds_client::{ExecuteOptions, PreparedStatement, ResultSet, ...}`) and never used (only occurrence in src/). `prepare_session(.., handle: &CancelHandle)` takes `handle` and does `let _ = handle;` at line 363, yet both call sites build and pass `&handle`. `SQL_HANDLE_DBC` (consts.rs:13) has one occurrence (its definition). connection.rs:155 `#[allow(unused_variables)]` on `new` hides unused `use_pool`/`token_factory`-style params.

title: RowBuffer::text and resolve_null_types parse sp_describe results with a per-call Vec<u16> and String clones
evidence: `conn.cached_param_types(sql)` returns `self.param_types.lock().get(sql).cloned()` (deep clone of Vec<(String,String)>) on every execute that has an untyped NULL, and `cache_param_types(sql, types.clone())` clones again on miss; the cache clears entirely at 512 entries (`cache.clear()`) causing a re-describe round trip storm; RowBuffer::text collects `Vec<u16>` per cell. Also `sql.replace('\'', "''")` + `format!` on every miss.
fix: Store `Arc<[(String,String)]>` (or Arc<Vec<..>>) in the cache so hits are a refcount bump; use a real LRU (e.g. evict oldest) instead of clear(); decode UTF-16 with `char::decode_utf16` over `chunks_exact(2)` without the intermediate Vec.
verify: The code matches the finding. `cached_param_types` deep-clones a `Vec<(String,String)>` on each hit. `cache_param_types` clears the whole cache at 512 entries. The miss path escapes the SQL and builds a `format!` string. All of this runs only when a statement has untyped NULL params. Each hit clones a handful of short strings, which is negligible next to the execute round trip. The miss path is dominated by the sp_describe network call. The clear-at-capacity cliff is real but needs more than 512 distinct NULL-bearing SQL texts on one connection. I did not check the `RowBuffer::text` Vec<u16> claim; it is minor either way. CONTRACT.md and upstream compatibility do not conflict with the fix. Switching to Arc and a simple eviction is cheap but low value, so this stays a nit.

title: Extra metadata round trip: sp_describe_undeclared_parameters per distinct SQL text for any None param
evidence: `let query = format!("EXEC sp_describe_undeclared_parameters @tsql = N'{escaped}'"); ... client.execute(query, ()).await?` runs on the first execution of each SQL text containing an untyped NULL, and the cache is keyed per ConnShared (`param_types: Mutex<HashMap<String, ..>>`) so every new pooled/short-lived connection repeats it; on pool checkout the same SQL is re-described. In the benchmark's loop-heavy paths (INSERT with None) this doubles round trips on cold caches.
fix: Make the cache process-wide keyed by (pool key/database, sql) so pooled connections share it, or fall back to sending NULL as `sql_variant`/untyped `NVARCHAR(1)` (what msodbcsql does for SQL_UNKNOWN_TYPE NULLs) and only describe on type-conversion error.
verify:
The mechanism is confirmed. resolve_null_types (src/statement.rs:283-330) runs `EXEC sp_describe_undeclared_parameters` once per SQL text that has an untyped None. The cache is a field of ConnShared (src/connection.rs:41). ConnShared is built fresh on every connect, including a pool checkout (connection.rs:206-221), so the cache is lost each time a pooled connection is reused. The code also matches docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:94 ("cached per SQL text per connection"), so this is deliberate design, not a bug. CONTRACT.md has nothing that forbids a wider cache.

Why I downgraded it:
- The cost is one extra round trip per (connection, SQL) pair. A long-lived connection that loops over the same INSERT pays it once. The "doubles round trips" claim only holds for cold, short-lived or pool-churned connections.
- The describe step exists for correctness. Untyped NULLs sent as nvarchar can fail against varbinary, datetime or other typed columns. The suggested fallback of sending sql_variant or NVARCHAR(1) and describing only on error is therefore risky, and it would change behaviour that the upstream tests rely on.
- A process-wide cache has a staleness problem. Results depend on schema and database, so the key would have to include pool key and database, and the cache would need invalidation after DDL. That is real churn for a niche win.

A process-wide cache keyed by (pool key, database, sql) is a reasonable later optimisation for pooled workloads. It is not a defect and should not block anything.

title: duckdb_over_arrow_3m has an odd `.fetchall().__len__()` and compare.py suppresses stdout/errors for failing drivers
evidence: `).fetchall().__len__()` instead of `len(...)`; and compare.py runs `subprocess.run(cmd, check=True, stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL)` so a benchmark that raises mid-way gives a CalledProcessError with no context, while stale `benchmarks/results/*.json` for non-selected drivers are silently reused and mixed into the table (`p.stem: json.loads(p.read_text()) for p in sorted(RESULTS.glob("*.json"))`, including results from a previous code revision).
fix: Use `len(...)`; let stderr through (already) but print the failing driver name on CalledProcessError; stamp results with git rev/timestamp and warn in the table when a reused file is from a different commit.
verify: Confirmed in code. bench_taxi.py:126 uses `.fetchall().__len__()`, which is stylistic only. compare.py:46 uses `check=True` with `stdout=DEVNULL`; stderr is not suppressed, so the traceback still shows and only the failing driver name is missing from the error. compare.py:48-50 globs every results/*.json, so with `--only` a stale file from a previous run or revision is mixed into the table without any warning. That can mislead a speedup comparison, but it is a dev-only benchmark script. Nothing in CONTRACT.md or upstream compatibility conflicts with it. The `len()` change and the driver-name message are trivial. Stamping results with the git rev is optional extra churn. Severity stays a nit.
